2.title: Fullness in Christ: Warnings Against Every Supplement
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is the letter’s most polemical section and its most theologically precise: the fullness that is in Christ alone (vv. 9–10) is set directly against every system that claims to supplement him. The chapter moves through three interlocking arguments. First (vv. 1–7): be rooted in Christ, built up in him, established in him — the metaphors of depth, growth, and stability describe the Christian who has genuinely understood what they have in him. Second (vv. 8–15): the Colossian philosophy is empty deceit; in Christ you have been circumcised with a true circumcision, buried and raised with him, forgiven all your trespasses, the law’s record of debt against you cancelled and nailed to the cross. Third (vv. 16–23): therefore let no one disqualify you by judging you on food, drink, festivals, new moons, or sabbaths — these are shadows; the substance is Christ. And the self-made religion that looks impressive is actually of no value against the indulgence of the flesh.

The theological heart of the chapter is verse 9–10: “in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him.” The fullness is Christ’s ongoing reality; the filling is the Colossians’ already-accomplished fact. Their fullness is given, settled, possessed. The false teachers are offering what the Colossians already have.

The legal image of verse 14 — “cancelling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands” — is one of the most vivid pictures of forgiveness in the New Testament. The image is of a written document of indebtedness, a bond or IOU, that records what is owed. God takes this document — the record of every sin, every violation, every debt we owe him — and nails it to the cross. The debt is not merely forgiven; the document is destroyed, posted publicly at the site of Christ’s execution, so that all can see: this debt has been paid in full, publicly, finally, at the cross.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Rooted and Built Up in Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul opens the chapter by letting the Colossians see the agony of his care. He is “struggling” for them — and for the Laodiceans, and for all who have never seen his face — wrestling in prayer for churches he never planted and never met, the very mark of a true shepherd’s heart. And what he longs for is not their ease but their establishment: that their hearts would be strengthened and braced, that they would be knit together in love, and that they would be brought to a rich, settled assurance — the confidence that comes from truly knowing God’s mystery, which is Christ himself, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are stored. Everything he wants for them funnels to one point: that they would know Christ deeply and be sure of him — for there is no wisdom worth having that is not already hidden in him.

Only now does Paul reveal why he has pressed the supremacy of Christ so hard: a danger is circling. False teachers would “delude” them with plausible arguments — and the peril is not that the error looks false but that it sounds like wisdom. Yet even from his prison cell, absent in body but present with them in spirit, Paul rejoices: their ranks are still in good order and their battle-line firm, their faith fixed on Christ. He commends a line that is holding before he moves to reinforce it — pastoral wisdom that fortifies the strong rather than only scolding the weak.

Then comes the heart of the section and the hinge of the whole letter: “as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him.” The way they began is the way they must go on — by faith, resting on Christ alone, never graduating past him to some “deeper” thing. Rooted in him like a tree in rich soil and built up on him like a house on bedrock, established in the very teaching they were first given, and overflowing with thanksgiving — for a heart full of gratitude for all it already has in Christ has no appetite for the counterfeit. Against every voice that whispers “Christ-plus,” this section answers with quiet force: you have him, he is enough, go deeper in.
verseByVerse.theology:
All the Treasures of Wisdom Hidden in Christ

Colossians 2:3 — “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” — is the epistemological foundation of the Reformed tradition’s approach to all knowledge. Cornelius Van Til’s presuppositionalism, Abraham Kuyper’s sphere sovereignty, Francis Schaeffer’s integrated Christian worldview: all are ultimately grounded in this text. All genuine wisdom and knowledge find their coherence and source in Christ. This does not mean that only Christians can know things; it means that all knowledge that is genuinely true is “thinking God’s thoughts after him,” participating (knowingly or not) in the structure of reality that Christ created and sustains. The Christian intellectual task is to follow wisdom wherever it leads, knowing that it leads ultimately to the one in whom all wisdom is hidden.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian philosophy offered esoteric wisdom that seemed to go beyond what the gospel provided. Paul says: all the wisdom you are seeking is already hidden in Christ. You are not lacking wisdom; you have not been exploring deeply enough the one in whom wisdom dwells. Now: The Christian who turns to secular philosophy, psychology, or spirituality for the wisdom that Christ supposedly cannot provide has accepted the false teachers’ premise. All genuine wisdom, wherever it is found, is a trace of the one in whom all wisdom is hidden. The Christian engages with every source of wisdom while recognizing that Christ is its ultimate source and criterion.

verseByVerse.quote: For I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you and for those at Laodicea and for all who have not seen me face to face,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you” — here is the heart of a true pastor. Paul lets the Colossians see straight into his inner life, and what they find is a man labouring for them. Then the astonishing detail: he struggles “for you and for those at Laodicea and for all who have not seen me face to face.” Paul had never been to Colossae; Epaphras planted the church (1:7). He had never met these people, would not have known them in the street — and yet he agonizes for them. That is a shepherd after Christ’s own heart: his care is not rationed to friends or converts who can repay him but reaches sheep in a valley he has never visited, simply because they belong to Christ. A hireling cares only for what the flock does for him; the true shepherd cares for the flock itself (John 10:12–13).

The word for “struggle” is agōn — the root of our “agony,” the all-out exertion of the wrestler in the contest, the same root he used of his ministry in 1:29. But notice his circumstances: he writes in chains (4:18), unable to visit or preach to them. So how does a caged apostle “struggle” for a church he cannot reach? Chiefly on his knees. His agony is the unseen labour of intercession — wrestling prayer, sleepless concern — exactly as Epaphras was “always struggling on your behalf in his prayers” (4:12). Pastoral love is not a warm feeling at a distance; it is hard, costly, hidden work, aimed at a goal: that their hearts be encouraged and brought to full assurance of Christ (v.2).

There is quiet comfort here for you, and a quiet summons. The comfort: somewhere, perhaps, an unseen saint is wrestling in prayer for you by name — the church is held up by hidden hands folded in prayer. And the summons: this is what love looks like — to care for another’s soul, even a soul you have never met, enough to labour for it before God (cf. Rom. 15:30; 2 Cor. 11:28).
verseByVerse.note: Laodicea lay about 10 miles from Colossae.

verseByVerse.quote: that their hearts may be encouraged, being knit together in love, to reach all the riches of full assurance of understanding and the knowledge of God’s mystery, which is Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verse 1 said Paul wrestles for these believers; verse 2 says what for — and notice what he does not ask. Not that they be wealthy, comfortable, or successful, nor even that the church grow in numbers, but three deeper things: that their hearts be strengthened, that they be knit together in love, and that they reach a rich, settled assurance in the full knowledge of Christ.

“That their hearts may be encouraged” — paraklēthōsin, not a pat on the back but to be braced, given courage to stand; and the “heart,” in the Bible, is the whole inner person. Why do they need it? Because the false teachers press in with plausible arguments (v.4), and a frightened, wavering heart is easily swept away, while a heart made sturdy can stand in the storm. This is the very strengthening the Spirit himself gives, for he is the Paraklētos, the Helper (John 14:16).

And Paul prays this not for solitary individuals but for hearts “knit together in love” (symbibasthentes) — parts woven and compacted into one body, the binding agent being the love “poured into our hearts” by the Spirit (Rom. 5:5). There is wisdom in joining the two: the lone sheep is picked off; the flock knit together stands. Heresy isolates and flatters the few; love weaves the whole body into one — and love is the very soil in which true understanding grows.

The summit is “all the riches of full assurance of understanding and the knowledge of God’s mystery, which is Christ.” “Full assurance” (plērophoria) is complete, settled confidence — faith brought all the way to certainty, not anxious or perpetually unsure — and it is assurance of understanding: not a leap in the dark but a confidence that rests on actually grasping the truth. And its goal is “the knowledge of God’s mystery, which is Christ” — for the mystery is not a secret doctrine but a Person (1:26–27); to know the mystery is simply to know Christ himself.

This is the death-blow to the heresy: the false teachers dangled “knowledge,” “mystery,” and “fullness” as prizes to be won beyond Christ, and Paul answers that the mystery is Christ, its riches already in him. For you this is pure comfort: God’s great desire is not that you be clever or initiated but that you be sure — rich in the settled, glad certainty of knowing the Lord Jesus (cf. Eph. 3:17–19; 2 Tim. 1:12).

verseByVerse.quote: in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“In whom” reaches back to the last words of v.2 — the mystery “which is Christ.” And in Christ, Paul says, “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.” Treasures — the precious things men dig and dive and travel the world to find. Wisdom and knowledge — between them the whole range of what the heart longs to grasp: knowledge, the understanding of God and reality; wisdom, the skill of living rightly in its light. And all of them are stored up in Christ. “Hidden” (apokryphoi) does not mean locked away from God’s people, but treasured up, kept safe — the way gold is kept in a vault. Christ is the strongroom in which God has stored everything worth knowing.

There is a sharp edge here, aimed at the false teachers. They peddled “hidden” wisdom — secret knowledge for the initiated few, reached by climbing past Christ into angel-speculation and mystical experience. Paul takes their prized word and turns it back: the truly hidden treasures — all of them — are hidden in Christ, not in any system of theirs. So there is no wisdom worth having outside of Christ, and no lack of it inside him. The Christian does not graduate from Christ to something higher; he goes ever deeper into Christ, who is himself the wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24, 30).

Two freeing things follow. First, you need not look anywhere else. You may quietly fear that the real riches belong to scholars and mystics, that you are a second-class believer outside the vault while cleverer people enjoy the gold. Not so — all the treasure is in Christ, and you have Christ; you already hold the key, and need only go further into the Saviour you already know. Second, the treasure has no bottom: a whole lifetime of knowing Jesus will not exhaust the riches stored in him.

Does this mean non-Christians can know nothing true? No. By God’s common grace unbelievers discover a great deal that is true, and Christians may learn from them. Paul is speaking of the wisdom that saves and makes sense of everything, which is found only in Christ.

Imagine a working man who spends years chasing rumours of treasure and signing up for one scheme after another — and then a lawyer tells him the deed to the richest mine in the country was made out in his name long ago. He already owns it; all his searching elsewhere was wasted effort; and the mine runs so deep a thousand lifetimes could never empty it. That is you and Christ (cf. Matt. 13:44).

verseByVerse.quote: I say this in order that no one may delude you with plausible arguments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With “I say this in order that…,” Paul reveals why he has pressed Christ’s all-sufficiency so hard: a danger is circling, and here he first names it plainly. Behind it lay what is often called the Colossian heresy — a mixture of Jewish rule-keeping (food laws, festivals, circumcision), harsh self-denial, the veneration of angels, and claims to secret knowledge. Its method was not to deny Christ outright but to add to him: Christ plus these rules, plus these mediators, plus this deeper experience.

“Delude you with plausible arguments.” “Delude” (paralogizētai) means to deceive by false reasoning — to talk someone out of the truth the way a swindler reasons a man out of his money. And “plausible arguments” (pithanologia) is the key: persuasive, reasonable-sounding speech. That is the whole peril — the error does not arrive looking obviously false; it comes dressed as wisdom (v.23), sounding sophisticated and convincing.

The pitch ran: “Faith in Christ is a fine beginning, but for real fullness you must also keep these days, deny the body, honour these powers, reach this higher knowledge.” The packaging changes; the pattern never does. Today the same voice says, “Jesus is essential, of course — but you also need this experience, this teacher’s system, these rules, to be truly filled.” The tell is always the little word plus: Christ is not quite enough; add something. Paul’s guard is simple — remember that all the treasures are already in Christ (v.3), and you will not be talked out of him (cf. 2 Cor. 11:3).

verseByVerse.quote: For though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing to see your good order and the firmness of your faith in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit.” Paul writes from a prison cell, to a church he has never even visited — and is “with them in spirit.” This is no mystical projection but the warm language of love that leaps over distance: his heart, thoughts, and prayers are genuinely with them (as in 1 Cor. 5:3). Beneath the affection lies a deeper truth — believers are bound together in Christ by one Spirit, and miles cannot sever that bond. For you it is quiet encouragement: the fellowship of the saints is not broken by distance, and one day the whole body will be gathered in one place at last.

And here is a man in chains, cut off from freedom and comfort — and the word that falls from his pen is rejoicing. Over what? Not his release or better conditions, but the spiritual health of a congregation he has never seen. Their faith was his joy. This lays bare a true shepherd’s heart: his deepest gladness lies not in his own circumstances but in the well-being of God’s people — “I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth” (3 John 4); “now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord” (1 Thess. 3:8).

He rejoices to see “your good order and the firmness of your faith in Christ” — both battlefield words. “Good order” (taxis) is troops drawn up in disciplined ranks; “firmness” (stereōma) is the solidity of a battle-line that holds, a fortress wall that does not give way. Picture an army standing in perfect order, ranks unbroken, holding firm against the assault — for the church is under attack (the plausible arguments of v.4), yet their line holds. This is why he commends them warmly before he warns them more sharply. And mark where the firmness comes from — “your faith in Christ”: their solidity is not self-manufactured grit but rests on its object, a line that holds because the One it leans on cannot be moved (cf. 1 Cor. 15:58; 16:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him, rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Therefore” is the hinge of the whole letter, gathering everything Paul has said and turning it into a command. Because Christ is supreme and all-sufficient, because in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom, because you received him and your faith stands firm — therefore here is what to do. Doctrine becomes duty: what is true of Christ grounds how you now live.

“As you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him.” Two things. What they received was not a set of teachings but a Person — “Christ Jesus the Lord,” received as Master, not an optional extra bolted onto the old life. And “walk” is the Bible’s word for the whole daily conduct of life. So the point is searching: the way you began is the way you go on. You came to Christ with empty hands, resting on him alone, receiving him by grace — so keep walking the very same way.

This is the death-blow to the heresy: the Christian life is not “receive Christ to get started, then graduate to higher teachings.” You do not move on from him; you go on in him — “having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?” (Gal. 3:3). However far you travel, you never leave the door you came in by: simple trust in Jesus.

“Rooted and built up in him” — and yes, Paul is mixing his metaphors: “rooted” is from the garden, a tree sunk deep into the soil; “built up” is from the building site, a house rising on its foundation. He stacks them cheerfully, as was normal in his world (Eph. 3:17; 1 Cor. 3:9), each adding something — and even the words differ in tense: “rooted” is settled and done (you have been planted in Christ, once for all), while “built up” is ongoing (you are being built, day by day).

Think of a great oak whose roots drive deep into rich soil, drawing all its life from that ground and standing unmoved through every gale — that is the believer rooted in Christ, the soil from which you draw your very life. And think of a house going up on bedrock, brick upon brick — that is the believer built up in Christ, founded on him and steadily growing. Anchored and rising, settled and growing.

And “just as you were taught” anchors them to what they first learned from Epaphras (1:7) — for the false teachers were doing the opposite, pulling them away from the original gospel toward something newer and supposedly deeper. The mark of truth is not novelty but faithfulness to what the apostles handed down; when a teaching promises more than the plain gospel of Christ you were first taught, that is precisely the moment to be on guard (Jude 3; 2 Tim. 1:13–14).

Finally, “abounding in thanksgiving” — overflowing, brimming over, no thin trickle but a flood. And it is no afterthought: a heart overflowing with thanks for all it already has in Christ has no appetite for the false teacher’s offer of “something more.” Ingratitude is the crack through which discontent creeps in, and discontent is exactly the foothold the heretic needs; gratitude bolts the door. But how fast we forget — Israel was fed with bread from heaven every morning and spent the journey murmuring, and we do the same, sitting on a mountain of grace while muttering about the weather and the bills.

So thanksgiving must be cultivated, deliberately, against the grain of a forgetful heart: stop, count the mercies, name them — a Saviour, sins forgiven, Christ living within you, the sure hope of glory — until the grumble shrinks. You will find it nearly impossible to grumble and give thanks in the same breath, so fill your mouth with the better of the two (cf. 1 Thess. 5:18; Col. 3:15–17).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Now the warning that has been gathering since the first chapter breaks into the open: “See to it that no one takes you captive.” The word is the kidnapper’s word — the false teaching is no harmless enrichment but an attempt to carry the Colossians off as plunder, by “philosophy and empty deceit” that rests on mere human tradition and on the “elemental spirits of the world.” Paul’s test cuts through every part of it with one phrase: “and not according to Christ.” Christ is the measuring rod. The believer does not need to master every error on offer; he needs to know the One by whom every error is exposed.

Against that hollow system Paul sets the towering reality of Christ — and of the believer in him. In Christ “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily”: not a portion of God parcelled out among spiritual intermediaries, but all of God, permanently, in the One who became flesh. And “you have been filled in him” — already complete, lacking nothing, joined to the One who is himself the head over every rule and authority. How complete? Paul presses it home with the language of death and resurrection.

In Christ they received the true circumcision “made without hands” — the whole old self cut away in his death; they were buried with him in baptism and raised with him through faith in the mighty working of the God who raised Jesus from the dead. The Christian does not begin with Christ and then climb beyond him; he has already died, been buried, and been raised in union with his Lord. There is no higher to go.

The section reaches its height at the cross. Once dead in trespasses and shut out as unclean outsiders, the Colossians were “made alive together with him” by sheer resurrecting grace, and forgiven all their trespasses, every last one. The certificate of debt that stood against us, with all its legal demands, God wiped clean and “set aside, nailing it to the cross” — the record of our guilt fastened to Calvary in the flesh of the crucified Son, carried into the grave, and left there paid in full.

And in the same stroke the powers the false teachers wanted the church to dread were stripped, shamed, and led away in chains: the cross that looked like Christ’s defeat was his triumphal procession, the principalities of darkness marched behind him as conquered prisoners. So the believer stands both complete and safe in Christ — nothing left to add, and no power left to fear. Everything the false teachers offer as a supplement has already been given, because nothing less than everything has been given in him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cancellation of the Debt and the Disarming of the Powers

Colossians 2:13–15 contains two of the most vivid metaphors for the atonement in the New Testament. First, the legal metaphor: the “record of debt” (cheirographon) that stood against us — the written bond of indebtedness, the document that recorded every sin and violation — has been cancelled, taken out of the way, nailed to the cross. The debt is not merely forgiven; the document is destroyed. Second, the military metaphor: the rulers and authorities who held humanity in their power through guilt and the law’s accusation have been “disarmed” and put to open shame — led in a triumphal procession like conquered enemies behind the victorious general. These two images together show what the cross accomplished: liberation from guilt (the debt cancelled) and liberation from spiritual bondage (the powers defeated).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian philosophy appealed to the elemental spirits and cosmic powers as real and threatening forces that needed to be placated through ritual observance. Paul says: those powers have been disarmed. They are defeated enemies, paraded in public shame behind the triumphing Christ. You do not placate them; you stand on the victory that has already been won. Now: The Christian who lives in fear of spiritual powers — who approaches life with anxiety about demonic influence, spiritual attack, or cosmic forces working against them — needs to hear this: the powers have been disarmed. Christ has triumphed. The fear of powers that have been publicly defeated is not piety; it is a failure to reckon with the victory of the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In v.4 Paul warned that someone might “delude” them; now he sounds the alarm and points at the enemy. “See to it” is a sharp watchman’s cry — Beware! — and he names the weapons of capture: philosophy, empty deceit, human tradition, the elemental spirits. “Takes you captive” (sylagōgōn) means to carry someone off as plunder, the picture of a slave-raider dragging away prisoners in chains. And here is the thing worth pondering: if a man tried to seize you physically and march you off in irons, everyone would see it and you would fight.

But when the kidnapping happens in the realm of ideas — when a teaching quietly carries off a person’s mind into bondage — almost no one notices, least of all the captive. He does not feel like a prisoner; he feels enlightened, thinks he is going “deeper,” being let in on something grand — while in truth he is being led away in chains. Spiritual captivity wears the disguise of progress, which is exactly why Paul shouts rather than whispers.

He names four weapons, overlapping and reinforcing one another. Philosophy (“love of wisdom”) — not all careful thinking (Paul reasoned with the philosophers at Athens), but this particular system, speculation that paraded as profound wisdom yet was hollow at the core. Empty deceit — the true verdict on it: it promises fullness and delivers a void, and it does not merely fail but misleads; mark the irony, it leaves a man empty while in Christ “you have been filled” (v.10).

Human tradition — trace its pedigree and it comes from men, not God, exactly what Jesus charged the Pharisees with: “you leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men” (Mark 7:8). And the elemental spirits of the world (stoicheia) — most likely the elemental spiritual powers thought to govern the world through the calendar and the stars, which men felt they must appease; to crawl back under them is to return to the slavery Christ broke (Gal. 4:3, 9).

“And not according to Christ” — these four words are the hinge, exposing the fatal flaw in all the rest. The teaching is according to philosophy, according to tradition, according to the elemental spirits — but not according to Christ, who is the measuring rod against which every idea is laid. And this is wonderfully freeing: you do not need to become an expert in every cult and master every false system to be safe. You need to know one thing surpassingly well — Christ.

Should Christians, then, avoid philosophy? No. Paul himself reasoned with philosophers (Acts 17:18–31). What he warns against is thought that takes people captive, according to human tradition and not according to Christ. Christians may and should study philosophy and every field of learning, testing all of it by Christ and his word.

A bank teller learns to spot forged notes not by memorizing every counterfeit ever printed, but by handling the genuine bill so constantly that anything false feels wrong the instant it touches his hand. So with you: know Christ deeply — his supremacy, his sufficiency, his finished work — and when a teaching diminishes him, adds to him, or sidelines him, you will feel the wrongness of it at once, however clever it sounds. The question is never merely “is this argument hard to answer?” but “is this according to Christ?” (cf. 1 John 4:1; Gal. 1:8).
verseByVerse.note: “Elemental spirits” may mean the basic principles of religion or the spiritual powers people believed ruled the world.

verseByVerse.quote: For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For in him” tells us this verse is the reason behind the warning of v.8. Why must the Colossians refuse capture and cling to Christ? Because — for — in him dwells the whole fullness of deity. That is the death-blow to every “Christ-plus” scheme: there is nothing to add to Christ, because all of God is already in him. And mark the stress: “in him,” in Christ and nowhere else — not in the angels, not in the powers, not in the impressive philosophy.

“The whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” — weigh every word. “The whole fullness” (pan to plērōma) — all of it, nothing left over, nothing residing elsewhere. “Of deity” (theotētos) is the strongest word available: not merely god-like qualities but Godhood itself, the very being and essence of God; Christ is not a creature filled with divine attributes but the One in whom the complete divine nature resides. “Dwells” (katoikei) is present tense and means to take up permanent residence — God at home in Christ, continually, even now in his exalted state. And the crowning word, “bodily” (sōmatikōs) — in a real human body: the incarnation at full stretch, the infinite fullness of God dwelling in the man Christ Jesus, flesh and all. All of God, in a body you could have stood beside.

This is the foundation of Paul’s whole case, and it strikes the false teachers from several sides. Against their angels and elemental spirits: if all the fullness of deity is in Christ, those powers have no fullness to offer — why seek lesser mediators? Against their scattered “fullness,” pictured as spread thin across a chain of beings: Paul says it is concentrated, entire and undivided, in Christ alone. And against their contempt for the body: that one word “bodily” rebukes every teaching that seeks God by escaping the physical, for God himself dwells bodily in Christ.

It also grounds the next line (v.10): because the fullness lives in Christ and you live in Christ, you have been filled — you lack nothing. To hunt for “more” beyond him is to turn from the fullness of God to chase empty shadows. In Christ you do not hold a fragment of God or a junior deputy; you have all of God there is to have (cf. 1:19; John 14:9).

verseByVerse.quote: and you have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The little word “and” carries us straight from Christ to ourselves: verse 9 said the whole fullness of deity dwells in him, and verse 10 draws the staggering inference — and you have been filled in him. Paul builds the word-link deliberately: the fullness (plērōma) dwells in Christ, and you have been filled (peplērōmenoi) in Christ — the same root. What is true of the Head overflows to the members.

Three things sit in “you have been filled in him.” The tense is a Greek perfect — a completed action with lasting results: not that you are slowly being filled or might one day be, but that you have been filled and remain full. It is passive: God filled you; you did not fill yourself. And it is “in him” — yours not by your own attainment but by union with Christ. Here is the hammer-blow to the heresy, which told the Colossians they were lacking and needed more rituals and experiences to reach fullness: you are already full in Christ; how can anyone add to fullness? (This does not mean you are sinlessly perfect or personally possess deity; it means you lack nothing for salvation, nothing for access to God, nothing for true completeness — it is all yours in Christ.)

And Christ is “the head of all rule and authority” — the source and sovereign over the spiritual powers, the very “rulers and authorities” the false teachers urged the church to revere. But Paul has said Christ created them (1:16) and will say he disarmed them at the cross (2:15); here he is their head. So the beings the Colossians were tempted to fear and flatter are themselves his subjects. Two great comforts follow, each aimed at the heresy.

First, you are complete: you may quietly feel like a second-rate Christian, sure the “real” believers have deeper experiences you are missing — but in Christ you have been filled; it is like a man with a fortune already in his account fretting that he is poor, when the answer is not to earn more but to wake up to what is already his. Second, you stand over the powers, not under them: you may carry your own vague dread of fate, of dark forces, of whatever pulls the strings behind life — and the One you belong to is the head over every power that exists. Not one of them outranks your Lord. There is nothing left to fear, and nothing left to add (Eph. 1:21–22; Rom. 8:38–39).

verseByVerse.quote: In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God, who raised him from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The false teachers were pressing the old physical rite of circumcision. Paul cuts the ground away: in Christ you have already received the true circumcision — not one “made with hands” by a human knife, but one “made without hands,” worked by God himself. And what is cut away is not a scrap of flesh but “the body of the flesh” — the whole old sinful self. This is what circumcision always pointed to; even in the Old Testament the real thing was “circumcision of the heart” (Deut. 30:6; Rom. 2:28–29). Paul calls it “the circumcision of Christ,” pointing to Christ’s own death, his being “cut off,” in which the believer shares. At the cross the old self was decisively cut away — and the Judaizer’s knife can add nothing to it.

He sets baptism beside it as a sign of the same reality. To go down into the water is to be “buried with him” — the old life not merely improved but put in the grave alongside Christ’s buried body (Rom. 6:3–4). And baptism does not stop at the grave: as the believer comes up out of the water, it portrays the next thing — “raised with him.” Union with Christ is union with his resurrection as well as his death: the old self buried, a new self raised to new life (the ground of 3:1, “if then you have been raised with Christ”). And mark how it happens — “through faith in the powerful working of God.” It is not the water that raises anyone, not the ritual working by itself, but the mighty power of God laid hold of by faith. Faith is the empty hand that receives; God’s power actually raises.

Paul says God raised Jesus — yet elsewhere the Spirit raised him (Rom. 8:11) and the Son raised himself (“I have authority… to take it up again,” John 10:18). This is no muddle but a window into the Trinity: the resurrection is the one, undivided act of the one God who is Father, Son, and Spirit. And here is the comfort folded in: the greatest display of power in history — the full might of the triune God raising Jesus — is the very power that raised you with him and is at work in you now (Eph. 1:19–20).

Why pile up circumcision, burial, baptism, and resurrection in the middle of a warning against false teachers? Here is the thread. They were saying, “You need more — be circumcised, keep our rules, climb higher.” Paul’s reply is to show what has already happened to you in Christ: you have received the true circumcision, the old self cut away by God; you have died and been buried with Christ, that chapter closed; you have been raised with him by the same power that raised Jesus from the grave. What, then, could anyone add? You cannot improve on death and resurrection.

Does baptism replace circumcision, so that the children of believers should be baptized? Christians who baptize infants argue so: circumcision was the sign of the covenant given to Abraham’s infant sons, and here Paul links it directly with baptism, so the new covenant sign belongs to believers’ children as the old one did. Those are serious arguments. But notice what Paul says: the circumcision he means is one made without hands, the inward work of Christ, and they were raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God. Paul does not say baptism replaces circumcision; he says Christ’s inward circumcision is what circumcision pointed to, and baptism is the sign of it, received by those who have faith. The more likely reading is that baptism belongs to believers.

Does baptism, then, save? Roman Catholic, Lutheran and some other Christians hold that God gives new birth through baptism. But Paul ties the raising to faith, not to the water. Baptism is more than a picture; it is God’s appointed sign and seal of union with Christ, and a public confession of it. But it does not work apart from faith. And the picture of burial and rising fits immersion most naturally, though Christians who pour or sprinkle see the washing as the main image.

This is the deep ground of “you have been filled in him” (v.10): when you trusted Christ you were so totally joined to him that everything he did became yours — his death your death, his resurrection your resurrection. The rites the heretics peddled are only shadows of a reality you already possess in full. So you are not half-finished or second-rate; you are one who has been through the grave and out the other side in Christ — now called to live as the raised person you already are (cf. Rom. 6:4–5; Col. 3:1–4).

verseByVerse.quote: And you, who were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses, by canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul does not say we were sick or struggling; he says we were dead — spiritual corpses, unable to respond to God or raise ourselves or contribute one thing to our own rescue (as in Eph. 2:1). He names two layers of the ruin: “in your trespasses,” sin the killer, the very thing we lay dead in; and “the uncircumcision of your flesh” — the Colossians were Gentiles, outside the covenant people, and deeper still, the phrase pictures the unrenewed heart with nothing yet cut away. We were doubly lost: dead in guilt, shut out as strangers.

“God made alive together with him” (one word in Greek, synezōopoiēsen) is resurrection language — God did for us exactly what he did for Christ in the tomb. Notice what it does not mean. Not that we were partly alive and God topped us up; the dead do not help raise themselves. Not self-improvement or turning over a new leaf — you do not improve a corpse, you raise it. And not that we earned it by a decision, for God made us alive even when we were dead (Eph. 2:5). This is grace at its purest: not God helping those who help themselves, but God giving life to those who had none.

“Having forgiven us all our trespasses” — the word (charisamenos) is built on the word for grace, and then comes the word to stop the heart: all. Not some, not the small ones, not only the sins up to the day you believed. All — past, present, and future; great and small; the ones you remember and the thousand you have forgotten; the secret ones no soul knows, and the scarlet ones that make you wince in the dark.

God did not pardon most and keep a private reserve of charges; he forgave all. There is no sin of yours lying outside this word — not the one that haunts you at three in the morning, not the one you have never confessed to a living soul, not the besetting sin you keep stumbling back into. And it is no cheap amnesty, no looking away; it is possible only because Christ bore every one of those sins himself (Ps. 103:12; Mic. 7:19).

Paul makes it vivid: God “canceled the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands.” The “record of debt” is one Greek word, cheirographon — a hand-written certificate of debt, an IOU signed by the debtor himself. Picture God keeping a ledger of all we owe him, every command broken, an itemized account “with its legal demands” standing in writing against us; that signed bond of guilt was the thing that condemned us, and the figures were beyond all paying. And God “canceled” it — the word (exaleiphō) means to wipe out, to wash the ink clean off the page: not deferred or reduced but erased, as though the debt had never been written (Isa. 43:25).

And he “set it aside, nailing it to the cross.” When the Romans crucified a man they nailed his charge-sheet above his head; over Jesus it read, “King of the Jews” (John 19:19). But Paul says it was our certificate of debt that was nailed up at Calvary — and press the question the picture raises: it was Jesus who was nailed there, so how was our record nailed with him? Because our debt was laid on him.

If all our trespasses are forgiven, past, present and future, why must Christians still confess sin? Because forgiveness has two sides. As our Judge, God has forgiven us once for all; there is no condemnation (Rom 8:1). As our Father, he still wants us to confess the sins that spoil our fellowship with him, and Jesus teaches us to pray daily, forgive us our debts (Matt 6:12; cf. 1 John 1:9). We confess not to stay saved, but because we are his children.

What was nailed to the cross? Some take it as the Mosaic law itself, which condemned; the more likely reading is that it is the record of our debt, our signed guilt before God’s law, which Christ cancelled by paying it. Either way, the law can no longer condemn those in Christ. That does not abolish God’s moral will: the ceremonial law is fulfilled, but love still keeps the commandments (Rom 13:8–10).

The document of our guilt did not drift to the cross on its own; it was fastened there in the flesh of the Son of God, who took our debt as his own and carried it into death. When the nails were driven through his hands, the bond that stood against us was driven through with them. He bore the charge-sheet that had your name on it and took it down into the grave — and it never came back out. The debt is not outstanding somewhere, waiting to resurface; it is buried in the tomb of Jesus, and the empty tomb is the receipt stamped “paid in full” (Isa. 53:5–6; Gal. 3:13).
verseByVerse.note: The “record of debt” was a handwritten certificate of debt signed by the debtor; the charge against a crucified man was nailed above him.

verseByVerse.quote: He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The “rulers and authorities” are not human kings but the spiritual powers — the fallen angelic and demonic beings, “the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12). These are the same powers Christ created (1:16) and rules as their head (2:10), and — crucially for Colossae — the very powers the false teachers were urging the church to fear and appease (the “worship of angels,” 2:18). They are real, personal, malevolent beings, and they held humanity in a threefold grip: as the powers behind our sin, as accusers wielding the law’s condemnation against us (the debt-record of v.14), and through the fear of death (Heb. 2:14–15). The Colossians lived under their shadow — and Paul announces that the shadow has been broken.

“He disarmed them” — the word means to strip off, as a soldier is stripped of his weapons. And what was the powers’ great weapon? Not brute force, but our sin and its just condemnation. The devil is “the accuser” (Rev. 12:10); his whole case rested on the unpaid debt of our guilt.

Now see how this verse is welded to the last: in v.14 God cancelled the debt and nailed it to the cross; in v.15 he disarms the powers — because the debt was their weapon. Once the record of guilt is wiped out and sin is fully paid, the accuser has nothing left to accuse with, the jailer has lost his keys, death has lost its sting. At the cross the weapon was wrenched clean out of their hands — and here is the deep irony: at Calvary it looked as though the powers had won, for they “crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8), but in that very act they were destroyed. Their apparent triumph was their undoing.

He also “put them to open shame” — made a public example of them, before the whole watching unseen world of angels and powers (and, through the gospel and the church, wider still, Eph. 3:10). And “by triumphing over them” uses the technical word for a Roman triumph (thriambeusas) — the victorious general parading into the city in his chariot, his conquered enemy kings dragged in chains behind him, stripped and displayed to the jeering crowds. Paul casts Christ as that triumphant General and the rulers and authorities as the captive kings shuffling behind his chariot. The cross, which the watching world saw as Christ’s shameful defeat, was in reality his victory parade — and the very instrument of death became the chariot of triumph.

This is the knockout blow of the whole argument. The false teachers told the Colossians they had to fear and appease these powers to be safe; Paul’s answer is devastating: the cross did not only forgive your sins (v.14) — it defeated the very powers you are being told to dread. Why bow to, or bargain with, or tremble before an enemy your own Lord has already conquered and led in chains? You may not fear “principalities” by that name, but you have your own dread of the unseen — of evil, of the devil, of dark forces working against you in the shadows.

To you Paul says the same: the powers of darkness are a defeated enemy. The devil is real, but he is beaten — disarmed, shamed, and chained behind the cross, like a fierce guard dog on a short chain who still barks and lunges and frightens the timid, but is bound and cannot drag down the one who belongs to the Victor. You are not called to fear the spiritual world or buy it off; you are called to stand in the finished victory of Christ (James 4:7; Rom. 16:20).
verseByVerse.note: A Roman general celebrated victory by parading his captives through the streets.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
With the great victory of the cross secured, Paul turns it into a charge: since the powers are disarmed, the debt cancelled, and you complete in Christ — let no one sit in judgment on you over food and drink, festivals, new moons, or sabbaths. He does not argue the merits of each rule; he reframes them all. These were “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.” A shadow is real and God-given — it traces the shape of what is coming — but once the body that casts it has arrived, to cling to the outline is not deeper piety; it is to turn from the person to his silhouette.

Paul then unmasks the false teacher himself. He would “disqualify” the Colossians, like a crooked umpire robbing them of a prize already theirs, unless they took up his program of self-imposed severity, the veneration of angels, and the parade of visionary experiences. It looks like humility and spiritual depth; in truth the man is “puffed up…by his sensuous mind” — the very flesh he claims to master is what inflates him. And beneath all the display lies the fatal flaw: he is “not holding fast to the Head.” For it is from Christ the Head, and from him alone, that the whole body is nourished, knit together, and grows with a growth that is from God. Cut off from the Head there is no life and no growth — only an impressive death.

Finally Paul lays the axe to the root of rule-religion. Since you died with Christ to the elemental principles of the world, why live as though you still belonged to it, submitting again to “Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch”? Such rules fuss over perishable things, rest on merely human commands, and — for all their impressive “appearance of wisdom” in self-made religion, asceticism, and severity to the body — are powerless to do the one thing they promise. They cannot curb the flesh; they only relocate it, feeding pride while starving the body. What austerity could never accomplish, union with the crucified and risen Christ already has. And that sets up the great turn of chapter 3: the answer to a dead religion of rules is not less effort but a new direction — upward, to the risen Christ, where the believer’s true life now is.
verseByVerse.theology:
Shadow and Substance: The Old Covenant as Anticipation

Paul’s description of the Mosaic observances as “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (v. 17) is the hermeneutical principle underlying all Reformed typological interpretation of the Old Testament. The ceremonial law — the festivals, the sabbaths, the food laws, the sacrificial system — was genuinely given by God and genuinely pointed forward to the reality that was coming. But it was always a shadow, not the substance; always anticipation, not fulfilment. The substance arrived in Christ. To return to the shadow when the substance is present is not faithfulness to the law; it is a failure to read what the law was always saying.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian teachers were using Jewish observances as part of their syncretic system, insisting that the Colossians needed to keep certain days and food laws and festivals. Paul says: these were shadows pointing to Christ; Christ has come. Now: The same principle applies to any Christian movement that makes Old Testament ceremonial practices the standard of Christian spirituality. The principles of justice, love, and holiness that the ceremonial law expressed are fulfilled in Christ and applied by the Spirit. The specific ceremonies have been fulfilled in him who was their substance all along.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Therefore” draws the conclusion from everything before it. Because you have been filled in Christ (v.10), because the record of debt was cancelled and nailed to the cross (v.14), because the powers have been disarmed (v.15) — therefore do not let anyone drag you back under a system of religious rules. What you are in Christ settles how you stand before these would-be judges.

The false teachers were pressing the Colossians to keep religious regulations — rules about clean and unclean food and drink, and the observance of sacred days: “festival… new moon… Sabbath” is the standard Old Testament summary of the Jewish sacred calendar (1 Chron. 23:31). And they were “passing judgment” — condemning the Colossians for not keeping these rules, making them feel second-class, disqualified. Paul forbids it flatly: your standing is in Christ, not in menus and calendars.

And there is a reason these things can no longer be made binding, which he gives next: they were “a shadow of the things to come” (v.17), signposts pointing forward to Christ — the rest the Sabbath pictured is found in him (Heb. 4:9–10), the feasts fulfilled at his cross. To make them a condition of acceptance is, in effect, to deny that Christ is enough. (Paul is not calling such observances sinful — a believer may hold his own convictions about days and food, Rom. 14 — but he will not let them be made the measure of anyone’s standing.)

The exact rules change; the dynamic never does. It is the same error whenever a secondary or man-made practice is made the measure of true spirituality and people are judged by it. It wears modern clothes: “a real Christian would never touch a drink”; you must follow this diet or fast to be holy; you must keep (or must not keep) Christmas or Lent; you must use only this Bible translation, sing only these songs, school your children in this one way.

Does this include the weekly Sabbath? Many Reformed Christians, following the Westminster Confession, hold that Paul means only the ceremonial sabbaths of Israel’s festivals, and that the weekly Sabbath remains a creation ordinance (Gen 2:3), now kept on the Lord’s Day. But Paul’s list, festival, new moon, Sabbath, is the Old Testament’s standard way of naming the yearly, monthly and weekly holy days together (cf. 1 Chr 23:31). The more likely reading is that the weekly Sabbath is included, a shadow fulfilled in Christ. Christians gather on the first day as a glad and ancient practice, but no day binds the conscience (Rom 14:5).

Wherever someone takes a matter Christ has left free and turns it into a test of whether you are accepted by God — and looks down on you for failing it — that is the Colossian heresy in a Sunday suit. And the rebuke cuts both ways: do not let anyone make you feel like a second-rate Christian over such things, and do not sit in judgment on a brother who differs from you (Rom. 14:1–4). This is no licence to despise all discipline — the gospel never frees us to sin, only from it. It is liberty of conscience: Christ alone is the ground of our acceptance, and no one may add a single rule to him (Gal. 5:1).

verseByVerse.quote: These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“These” — the food laws and holy days of v.16 — are “a shadow.” Think what a shadow is: the dark outline an object throws, with the shape of the thing but none of its substance; you cannot shake a shadow’s hand. The whole ceremonial law was exactly that — a God-given shadow cast ahead of a coming reality, and the reality it traced was Christ. The Passover lamb outlined the Lamb of God; the Day of Atonement outlined his once-for-all sacrifice; the Sabbath outlined the rest he gives; the tabernacle outlined God come to dwell with his people. A shadow is real and useful — it truly tells you something is on its way — but was never meant to be clung to as though it were the thing itself (Heb. 10:1).

“But the substance belongs to Christ.” The word for “substance” is literally body (sōma), and the contrast is beautiful: the shadow (skia) set against the body that casts it. The solid body that threw this entire shadow-play — the whole Old Testament system — is Christ himself. And once the body has arrived, you do not go on clutching the shadow: when your friend walks through the door, you do not keep staring at his silhouette on the wall. To return to the ceremonial rules now that Christ has come is to prefer the outline to the person. So you have lost nothing by leaving the shadows behind — you have gained the very One they were all pointing to. Every feast and sacrifice was a finger tracing the shape of Jesus before he came; now that he has come, the finger has found what it was pointing at (Matt. 5:17; John 5:39).

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one disqualify you, insisting on asceticism and worship of angels, going on in detail about visions, puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Let no one disqualify you” — the word (katabrabeuō) comes from the games: the umpire who awards the prize, and to disqualify someone is to rule against him and rob him of it. The false teachers set themselves up as umpires over the Colossians’ faith, pronouncing them out of the running unless they took up the teachers’ program. Paul’s reply: do not let anyone rob you of a prize already yours in Christ. And the program had three strands.

First, asceticism. The Greek says the false teacher “delights in humility” — but a twisted humility: self-imposed severity toward the body, rigorous fasting and harsh self-denial, treating the body roughly as a path to higher spirituality (named again in v.23, “severity to the body”). It looked humble, even impressive, but was a performance of lowliness, not the real thing. (This is no attack on genuine self-discipline or fasting, which Scripture commends; it is the turning of bodily severity into a badge of rank.) Second, worship of angels — giving religious devotion to angelic beings as mediators and guardians, channels through which to approach God.

The error is plain: it dethrones the one Mediator between God and men (1 Tim. 2:5) and bows to the very powers Christ is head over (2:10); angels themselves refuse it — when John fell to worship one, the angel said, “You must not do that… worship God” (Rev. 19:10). Third, going on in detail about visions — the teacher paraded “the things he had seen,” mystical experiences won through his disciplines, and built his authority from them: “I have seen what you have not; follow me and you can too.” It was spiritual one-upmanship by experience, making private revelations rather than Christ and his Word the measure of who is advanced.

Now Paul lances it: for all the impressive display, the man is simply “puffed up” — swollen, inflated with pride — and “without reason,” groundlessly, for there is nothing actually there. And the killing stroke: he is puffed up “by his sensuous mind,” literally “the mind of his flesh.” Here is the irony at the heart of it: the man who beats his body to escape the flesh, who scales the heavens in visions to rise above it, is driven the whole time by the flesh — by the fallen nature’s craving for status and superiority.

The austerity feeds his pride; the visions feed his self-importance; his “humility” is vanity in disguise. All three strands are still with us — holiness equated with severity, the fascination with angels and “spirit guides” and other mediators slipped between the believer and Christ, the experience-chasing that rates a Christian by his dramatic encounters. Beneath them all runs the same error: a spiritual elite making ordinary believers feel disqualified unless they add some practice or experience to Christ — and, underneath the show, the same fleshly pride. The safeguard, in every age, is the next verse: hold fast to the Head (cf. 1 Cor. 8:1).
verseByVerse.note: The false teaching seems to have mixed Jewish rules, strict self-denial and fascination with angels and visions.

verseByVerse.quote: and not holding fast to the Head, from whom the whole body, nourished and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with a growth that is from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Not holding fast to the Head” — “holding fast” means to grip tightly, to cling, and “the Head” is Christ (as in 1:18; 2:10). So in a single phrase is Paul’s diagnosis of the whole heresy: for all his visions and disciplines and angel-talk, the false teacher has let go of Christ. He has shifted his grip — from the Saviour to rules, experiences, and spiritual beings — and that is fatal, because everything depends on keeping hold of the Head. It is the exact opposite of the healthy believer “rooted and built up in him” (2:7), and it implies our part: hold on, do not drift, do not loosen your grip when something newer and more impressive comes along.

“From whom the whole body… grows.” Christ is the Head, the church his body, and from the Head — and nowhere else — the whole body draws its life. Paul fills in the anatomy: the body is “nourished” (fed) and “knit together” (bound into one) “through its joints and ligaments,” the connecting tissues that both link the parts and carry the supply down from the head to every limb. Life flows from Christ the Head, through all the connections, into every member, so that the body is at once fed and held together — and therefore grows. And the growth “is from God”: the increase is his own doing, not something the body manufactures by technique (Eph. 4:15–16; 1 Cor. 3:6–7).

Here is the whole thing in a picture. Cut a branch from the vine and it does not grow — it withers, because all the life was in the vine (John 15:5); sever a hand from the arm and no exercise will make it grow. That is exactly what the false teachers were unwittingly doing: by drawing people off Christ onto their rules and visions, they were cutting the branch from the vine, offering a fancier life while severing it from its only source. So two things.

First, your growth is not a technique to master but the natural fruit of staying joined to Jesus; your job is to hold fast to the Head — close to Christ in faith, the Word, and prayer — and God himself supplies the increase. Stop hunting for life in programs and rule-keeping; stay gripped to Christ, and you will grow. Second, you do not grow alone: you grow as part of the body, knit to other believers, the life of the Head running through the connections. A Christian was never meant to be a severed limb.

verseByVerse.quote: If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world, why, as if you were still alive in the world, do you submit to regulations— “Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch” (referring to things that all perish as they are used)—according to human precepts and teachings? These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world” — the “if” is not a doubt but a settled fact: since you died with Christ. The “elemental spirits” (stoicheia, as in v.8) are the basic governing principles and powers of the old order — the whole system of religious rules and the forces behind it. And Paul says you died to all of it: united to Christ in his death (2:11–12), you were severed from that old regime and released from its jurisdiction, for death dissolves every old bond (Rom. 7:1–6). The elemental rules have no more claim on you than a master has on a slave who has died. So to take up that world’s regulations again is to behave “as if you were still alive in the world” — as if the death had never happened. It is a freed slave voluntarily walking back into the slave-quarters and picking up his old chains.

Paul even quotes the slogans of the system — “Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch” — and notice their character: every one a prohibition, a religion of forbiddings, and pettily piled up (“touch” is lighter than “handle,” so even the faintest contact is banned). Then he lets the air out of the whole thing. The things these rules agonize over — foods and the like — are perishable; they “perish as they are used,” eaten and gone, and cannot touch the soul (as the Lord said, what enters the stomach does not defile the heart, Mark 7:18–19). And they come “according to human precepts and teachings” — man-made, not the commands of God, the very phrase Jesus flung at the Pharisees: “teaching as doctrines the commandments of men” (Mark 7:7; Isa. 29:13). Rules God never gave cannot bind a soul God has freed.

Paul grants that “these have indeed an appearance of wisdom” — they look wise, rigorous, deeply spiritual; the fasting looks like devotion, the strict rules like holiness, the severity like depth. That is exactly their danger: a convincing surface with no reality beneath. Three things give the show its impressive look — “self-made religion” (a word found nowhere before Paul, ethelothrēskia, “will-worship”: worship a man chooses for himself rather than God commands), paraded “humility,” and merciless “severity to the body.” It all looks magnificent, but the coined word exposes the root: self-will dressed up as devotion.

And then the verdict that brings it all down: it is “of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh.” For all the show, the system fails at the one thing it claims to do — it cannot curb sin. External prohibition does not conquer the flesh; it only relocates it. Starve the body, and the flesh does not die; it grows fat on pride, swelling with self-righteous satisfaction in its own discipline. Rules can trim outward behaviour but cannot change a heart, and may even inflame the very sin they forbid (Rom. 7:5–8). The flesh is defeated not by a rule-book but only by death and resurrection with Christ — which is exactly where Paul turns next (3:1–5). So here is his point in plain words: you died with Christ to the old world of rule-keeping, so do not crawl back under man-made rules as though you still belonged to it.

Does this make fasting and self-discipline pointless? No. Jesus expected his disciples to fast (Matt 6:16–18), Paul says I discipline my body and keep it under control (1 Cor 9:27), and bodily training is of some value (1 Tim 4:8). What Paul condemns is rules imposed as the way to holiness or acceptance with God. Discipline as a means of growth, done in faith, is good.

Such rules — don’t handle, don’t taste, don’t touch — look wise and holy, and are dangerously attractive; but they are invented by men, they fuss over perishable things that cannot touch the soul, and — the fatal flaw — they have no power whatever to make you holy. They are like cutting weeds off at ground level: the garden looks tidy for a day, but the roots are alive and the weeds come straight back. Only Christ digs out the root. The cure for sin is not a tighter rule-book; it is a living Saviour — and you have died and been raised with him, so the way forward is not to climb back under the rules but to hold fast to the Head and live the new life from above, which is exactly what chapter 3 will unfold (cf. Rom. 8:13; Gal. 5:16).
