3.title: Set Your Minds on Things Above: The Old and the New
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is the ethical consequence of everything chapters 1–2 have established. The logic is characteristically Pauline: because of who you are in Christ (indicative), live accordingly (imperative). You have died with Christ; you have been raised with Christ; your life is hidden with Christ in God; Christ is your life. Therefore: set your minds on things above, put to death what is earthly in you, put off the old self, put on the new self — and let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, the word of Christ dwell in you richly, and everything you do be done in the name of the Lord Jesus.

The chapter’s structure is the structure of the gospel applied to daily life: the negative movement of putting off (vv. 5–11), and the positive movement of putting on (vv. 12–17). The things to be put off are the practices of the old self — sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, covetousness, anger, wrath, malice, slander, obscene talk, lying. The things to be put on are the character of the new self — compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, patience, forbearing one another, forgiving each other, and above all, love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony.

The chapter then extends this transformation into the household (vv. 18–4:1): the practical ordering of the most intimate human relationships — wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters — under the lordship of Christ. These are not arbitrary social regulations; they are the gospel working its way into the fabric of daily life, the supremacy of Christ (chapter 1) arriving at the breakfast table, the bedroom, and the workplace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Set Your Minds on Things Above
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Chapter 3 turns from what the believer must not do (the rule-religion demolished in chapter 2) to a wholly new direction. “If then you have been raised with Christ” — and the “if” means “since”: the resurrection with Christ is an accomplished fact. The believer has already been raised, here and now — he need not climb a single rung through fasting, visions, or angels to reach the heavenly realm, for in Christ he is already there.

From that ground come two commands that reach the whole inner person: seek the things above (the bent of desire and pursuit) and set the mind on them (the settled orientation of thought). This is no mystical escapism that despises the body, the job, or the home — it is the reordering of the entire life around the risen, reigning Christ, the way an exile lives and works in a foreign land with his heart fixed on home, for “our citizenship is in heaven.”

And the things above are not the celestial geography of the false teachers; they are wherever Christ is — “seated at the right hand of God,” the place of supreme honour and finished work, the very powers the Colossians feared now beneath his feet. The crucified one is the crowned one, and he reigns there as the believer’s own representative and advocate. Why seek what is above? Because that is where the believer’s true life now is: “you have died” (the old self buried with Christ) and “your life is hidden with Christ in God” — at once safe, locked in the most secure place in the universe, beyond the reach of any enemy, and hidden, not yet on display.

For the hiddenness has an appointed end. “When Christ who is your life appears” — he does not merely give life; he is our life — “then you also will appear with him in glory.” The ordinary, unremarkable believer, like an heir who has lived his whole life unrecognised, will be led out and revealed in glory beside the King on the day of his coming. That certain future is the great motive for present holiness, and it carries the whole section that follows.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Hidden Life and the Security of the Believer in Christ

Colossians 3:3 — “your life is hidden with Christ in God” — is one of the New Testament’s most comprehensive statements of the security of the believer. The life of the Christian is not exposed to the attacks of the world, the flesh, or the devil in any ultimate sense; it is hidden, concealed, kept safe in the most secure location possible: with Christ, in God. Reformed theology has always grounded assurance of salvation not in the believer’s performance but in the security of their position: in Christ, kept by God. This is why the Christian can face the world’s hostility and the flesh’s internal rebellion without ultimate despair; the life that matters is in a place nothing can reach.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being told that their spiritual security depended on correct navigation of the angelic hierarchy, proper observance of festivals and food laws, and achievement of special spiritual states. Paul says: your life is hidden with Christ in God. There is no spiritual power that can reach it; no ritual failure that can revoke it; no ignorance of esoteric knowledge that can diminish it. Now: The Christian whose sense of security rises and falls with their spiritual performance — who feels secure on days of devotional discipline and insecure on days of failure — needs to hear this: your life is hidden. It is not at risk. It is kept by the one whose power infinitely exceeds every force that would threaten it.

verseByVerse.quote: If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“If then” turns the argument. All through chapter 2 Paul pulled down the rule-bound, ascetic religion of the false teachers, ending with the verdict that such things are powerless against sin (2:20–23). Now the positive alternative. He has been working two halves of one truth: “if you died with Christ” frees you from the world’s rules (2:20); “if then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things above.” The cure for a failed religion of rules is not no effort and no direction, but a new direction — not down into severity to the body, but up toward the risen Christ. The Christian life is not asceticism but aspiration. And the “if” means since (the same construction as 2:20): Paul is not asking whether they belong to Christ but building his command on the fact that they do.

“Raised with Christ” is not a promise about the distant future but a statement of what has already happened. United to Christ (2:12), you share his resurrection now; the same almighty power that rolled the stone away has raised you to new life. You are not waiting to be made alive someday — in Christ you are already as truly raised as your Lord is raised, because his resurrection is your own. And see how this answers the heresy: the false teachers urged the Colossians to climb — through fasting, visions, angels — to reach the heavenly realm; Paul says they need not climb a single rung, for in Christ they have already been raised there (Eph. 2:5–6).

“Seek the things that are above” is a present command — keep seeking, keep pursuing, keep making Christ’s kingdom your aim and your treasure. But it does not mean floating in mystical detachment, despising your job or family or daily life — that would be the very escapism Paul just condemned. It means the reorientation of the whole bent of your life — desires, aims, treasure, ambition — around the risen Christ rather than the passing things of earth. The one who seeks the things above still drives his van and pays his bills, but he does it all for Christ; it is a matter of what he finally lives for — “where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matt. 6:21).

And Paul locates “the things above” with precision: they are “where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God” — the place of supreme honour and finished work, for Christ sat down there, his saving work complete (Ps. 110:1; Heb. 1:3). The Christ you are told to seek is no dead teacher or distant ideal but the living, enthroned Lord of the universe, with the very powers the false teachers feared beneath his feet (2:15). Let it land: the same Jesus who hung on the cross bearing your debt now sits on the throne of heaven — the crucified one is the crowned one — and he is yours, reigning there as your representative and advocate (Rom. 8:34).

verseByVerse.quote: Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verse 2 deepens verse 1: there Paul said “seek”; here, “set your minds” — another ongoing command, meaning more than passing thought. It is the settled bent of the mind, the whole orientation of one’s thinking and valuing (the same word as “have this mind among yourselves,” Phil. 2:5). Whatever you habitually dwell on and prize, set that on the things above; aim the thoughts upward, and the life will follow. And the counterweight is deliberate — “not on things that are on earth,” the perishable things treated as ultimate (the possessions and priorities of the old order, and the very sins of v.5). The two cannot both be the mind’s true north: a mind set on earth makes an earthbound man; a mind set above makes a heavenly-hearted one (Rom. 8:5–6).

This is easily taken the wrong way, so be clear. It does not mean becoming so heavenly-minded you are no earthly good, nor despising your body, your work, or honest pleasures (that is the asceticism Paul just demolished), nor drifting through life in a mystical haze. Of course you must still think about your job, your bills, your garden — that is right and godly, and Paul will give very down-to-earth instructions about home and work in a few verses.

The question is what your mind is finally set on: what you treasure, what governs you, what you interpret all of life by. Think of an Englishman living and working abroad — he does his job and pays his way, but his heart is set on home, and everything he does is coloured by where he truly belongs. So it is with you: “our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). Live and labour on earth with your heart set on home — on Christ, and the kingdom that will never perish.

verseByVerse.quote: For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For” gives the ground beneath the command. Why seek and set your mind on things above? Because “you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” — your very life is located above, with Christ, so of course you should seek what is above, where your life actually is. The two truths of the new self are now complete: you have been raised with Christ (v.1), so you reach upward; and you have died (v.3), so the old earthbound life is behind you.

“You have died” is a finished fact: in union with Christ’s death, the old you — the self that belonged to the world and lived for its things — has died and been buried with Christ (Rom. 6:2–6). That is why you no longer set your mind on earthly things as your treasure: the man who lived for them is dead, and a new self has been raised in his place. And “your life is hidden with Christ in God” carries two glorious senses at once.

First, hidden means safe: your life is stored away, locked in the most secure place in the universe — double-wrapped, your life in Christ and Christ in God — so that no enemy, no sin, no devil, not death itself can reach in and snatch it (John 10:28–29). Second, hidden means concealed: your true life and glory are not on display yet. The world cannot see it, and for now it looks ordinary, unremarkable, often weak — but hidden is not lost; it is stored, waiting for the day it will be unveiled (v.4).

This may read like high mysticism, yet it is the most down-to-earth comfort a struggling believer could have. First, you are utterly secure: your real life — your salvation, your standing with God, your very self — is not held in your own trembling hands but locked away with Christ in God. On your worst day, when you feel a failure and a fraud, your life is still safe, because it hangs not on your performance but on Christ. Second, you are not yet what you will be.

Right now you may look like nothing much — ordinary, aging, weary — and feel no glory in yourself; that is because your real life is hidden for now, like a seed buried in winter ground, like an acorn that does not yet look like the oak. But the glory is real and it is coming: when Christ appears, what is hidden will burst into the open. So lift your head — you do not have to achieve your life, guard it, or prove it; it is kept safe with Christ in God (cf. 1 John 3:2).

verseByVerse.quote: When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having spoken of present realities — you have been raised, you have died, your life is hidden — Paul now lifts the eyes to the future, to the day of Christ’s return. This is the capstone of the paragraph and the answer to its deepest “why”: your life is hidden with Christ now, and it will not stay hidden — when he appears, it will blaze into the open in glory. The pattern is hidden-now, revealed-then. And the verse is the hinge of the argument, for having settled who you are and will be, Paul is about to draw the practical conclusion — “Put to death therefore…” (v.5). Future glory is the great motive for present holiness.

Notice the breathtaking phrase: “Christ who is your life.” Paul does not say Christ merely gives us life, as though it were a gift we hold apart from him; he says Christ is our life — its source, its substance, its very centre. He is not an addition to your life, one good thing among many; he is your life. (This is the final answer to a heresy that offered Christ-plus: Christ is not part of the package; he is the whole of it — Gal. 2:20; Phil. 1:21.) And “when Christ appears” — the word means to be brought out of hiding into open view. Right now he is hidden, enthroned at God’s right hand, unseen by the world; but a day is fixed when he will be revealed in glory before the whole creation. Mark the word “when,” not “if”: his appearing is certain; only the hour is unknown.

“You also will appear with him in glory.” Here your destiny is bound fast to Christ’s: as your life is now hidden with him, so it will be revealed with him — and not in shame but in glory. The hidden life of v.3 will be displayed at last, and you, who look like nothing much now, will shine with the very glory of Christ, transformed into his likeness (1 John 3:2; Rom. 8:17–18). Strip it down and it is the surest, most thrilling future a person could have. Right now you are hidden — plain, weary, unremarkable, often struggling.

But a day is fixed when Christ will burst into view, and on that day you will burst into view with him, sharing his glory; what you truly are will finally be seen. Think of an heir to a great throne who has lived his whole life unrecognised, in working clothes, and the day of the coronation comes: he is led out, robed, and revealed before all as the king’s own son. That is you. You do not have to earn this glory or guard it — it is fixed and certain, tied to Christ’s own appearing, which cannot fail. Your story does not end in the grave or in obscurity; it ends in glory, with Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–11 — Put to Death, Put Off
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The imperative flows straight from the indicative: because you have died with Christ (v. 3), put to death what is earthly in you (v. 5). The word is violent — kill, execute — for sin is an enemy to be slain, not a pet to be tamed; yet this is no return to chapter 2’s flesh-punishing rules, which cannot touch the heart. It is mortification by the Spirit, from a standing already secured: become what you already are. The first list of sins runs from the outward deed inward to the desire — immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire — climaxing in covetousness, which Paul flatly names idolatry, the craving that sets created things where God alone belongs. Such sins are no trifles: the wrath of God is coming against them, and they were the very air the Colossians once breathed — though that life is now decisively past.

So Paul turns to a second image: “put them all away,” strip them off like filthy clothes — the anger that smoulders, the wrath that flares, the malice beneath both, the slander and the obscene talk that empty a corrupt heart through the mouth. And the deep ground of it all is stated twice: “you have put off the old self” and “have put on the new self.” The change of clothing has already happened, once for all, in Christ; the daily putting-off and putting-on simply live out an accomplished reality. Meanwhile that new self “is being renewed” — an ongoing work of God — “in knowledge after the image of its creator”: sanctification is nothing less than the restoration of the defaced image of God, the patient cleaning of a painted-over portrait until the likeness of Christ shines out again.

And this new self is corporate as well as personal. In it the great walls of the old humanity — race, religion, culture, class, down to the most despised Scythian — no longer divide; they are not erased as facts but dethroned. “Christ is all, and in all”: the one thing that finally defines a person is whether Christ is his, and the same indwelling Christ in every believer is what makes them one.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mortification: Putting to Death What Christ Has Already Condemned

John Owen’s great treatise Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers is the most sustained Reformed treatment of what Paul commands in Colossians 3:5. Owen’s central principle — “be killing sin, or it will be killing you” — reflects Paul’s logic exactly. The mortification Paul calls for is not the ascetic self-punishment that the Colossian false teachers practiced and Paul has just condemned (2:23); it is the Spirit-enabled application of the cross to specific sinful desires, the practical reckoning with what Christ accomplished: these desires belong to the old self that died in Christ; by the Spirit I put them to death.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being offered an ascetic program that promised to deal with the flesh by external denial. Paul says: that program has no value in stopping the flesh’s indulgence (2:23). The real program is mortification — not external prohibition but the internal death-dealing of the Spirit to specific desires. The difference is not severity (asceticism can be more severe than mortification) but source: mortification flows from union with the crucified Christ. Now: The Christian who is fighting sin through willpower and self-discipline alone is using the wrong weapons. Mortification is spiritual warfare: the application of Christ’s death to specific sin patterns, in prayer, by the Spirit, in the community of faith. The fight is real; the weapon is the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Put to death therefore” reaches back to vv.1–4: because you have died and been raised with Christ, because your life is hidden with him and will appear with him in glory — therefore put the old sins to death. This is the great pattern of the Christian life: become what you are. You died to the old life as a finished fact (v.3); now daily put to death its lingering expressions. And note the contrast with chapter 2: this is not the asceticism Paul just condemned — rules imposed from outside, which cannot touch the flesh (2:23) — but the killing of sin from the inside, by those already dead-and-raised with Christ.

The word (nekroō) is violent: kill, execute. Not manage, not tame, not go easy on — kill. Sin is an enemy to be executed, not a pet to be domesticated. What is to be killed is “what is earthly in you” — the sinful desires and habits of the old nature that still cling to the believer. And how? Here is the handle: it is a paradox with v.3 — you have died with Christ once for all, yet you must put sin to death daily, and the finished fact is exactly what fuels the ongoing fight.

The killing is done not by flesh-punishing rules but “by the Spirit” (Rom. 8:13), in the strength of God, and from the standing of one who already belongs to Christ. In practice you name the sin as the enemy it is, refuse it, starve it, flee the temptation, say a decisive and ruthless no — leaning the whole way on the Spirit’s power, not gritting your teeth to earn God’s favour but fighting from a favour already yours. Be killing sin, or it will be killing you.

Paul names five, and the order digs from the outward act down to the inward root. Sexual immorality (porneia) is the broad word for every sexual act outside marriage — the outward deed. Impurity (akatharsia) moves inward — the defiled imagination and polluted inner life. Passion (pathos) goes deeper — the ungoverned lust that masters a person. Evil desire (epithymia kakē) reaches the very bottom — the wrong craving of the heart itself. Paul is exposing something vital: sin is not merely bad behaviour to be tidied on the surface; it runs all the way down into what the heart wants — which is why rules alone can never cure it; they trim the deed and leave the desire alive.

And he crowns the list with a startling word: “covetousness, which is idolatry.” Covetousness (pleonexia) is greed — the restless craving for more — and Paul calls it flatly what it is: idolatry. Why? Because to covet is to set the heart’s supreme desire and trust on something other than God, looking to created things for the security and worth God alone can give; whatever a man treasures above God is his functional god, and the greedy man bows at the altar of his own wallet (Eph. 5:5; Matt. 6:24).

It climaxes the list because it lays bare the idolatry beneath all these sins — every one is, at root, seeking in something other than God the life that only God can give. And it is the sneakiest of sins, for it wears a respectable coat: just “wanting a bit more,” just “a nicer life.” The cure is the whole chapter’s: when Christ himself is your life (v.4), the idols lose their grip (Luke 12:15).

verseByVerse.quote: On account of these the wrath of God is coming.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Between the two lists of sins (v.5 and v.8) Paul pauses to give the reason they must be killed and stripped off: “On account of these the wrath of God is coming.” Why deal so ruthlessly with these sins? Because they are exactly what God’s judgment is set against — the wrath of God is the dark backdrop that makes putting sin to death not optional but urgent. And that wrath is not a bad temper, a petty loss of control, God flying off the handle. It is the settled, holy, righteous opposition of a perfectly good God to all evil — his just, judicial reaction against sin.

Far from a flaw, it is the necessary mark of his goodness: a judge who felt no opposition to injustice would be no good judge, and a God indifferent to evil would be no good God. And it “is coming” — real, and on its way, a day of judgment fixed (Rom. 2:5). These sins, then, are no trifles to be excused or kept as pets; they are the very things divine judgment is advancing against. For the believer there is deep sobriety here, and deep relief: this is the very wrath that fell on Christ in our place (2:14), so that we are rescued from the wrath to come (1 Thess. 1:10) — all the more reason not to go back and dabble in what cost the Saviour so much (cf. Eph. 5:6; Rom. 1:18).

verseByVerse.quote: In these you too once walked, when you were living in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“In these you too once walked, when you were living in them.” Paul is not claiming that every person outside Christ commits every sin on the list, or that all are equally vile — people apart from Christ differ enormously, and many are outwardly decent and restrained, for God’s common grace holds back the full flood of sin in the world. He is saying two things. First, this was the Colossians’ own former life: they “once walked” (it was their habitual road) in these very sins, when such things were the element they lived and breathed in.

Second, and more deeply, these sins are the native air of life apart from God — the realm the old life belongs to, its natural tendency and fruit, whether or not every sin shows its face in every person; the unredeemed heart is turned from God at the root (1:21), and this is the direction that turning runs. And notice the tender “you too” — even you, now God’s holy people, were once in this. It is meant to keep the believer humble (do not look down on those still trapped; you were there yourself) and grateful (grace reached in and lifted you out). And it sets up the great pivot of v.8: once you walked there — but now. That was your old country; you have emigrated; do not move back (cf. 1 Cor. 6:11; Titus 3:3–5).

verseByVerse.quote: But now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But now you must put them all away” — the great hinge from the old life to the new. Where v.5 said kill (sin as an enemy to be executed), v.8 says take off — like stripping off filthy, stinking clothes and throwing them aside. Same call to deal decisively with sin, under a new image. But how, when you have tried so often to “just stop” and still struggle? Here is the help. This is not mere white-knuckle willpower in your own strength — that is the chapter-2 asceticism that cannot conquer the flesh. Putting off always comes paired with putting on (vv.10, 12): you overcome a sin not by leaving a hole where it was but by replacing it — take off anger and put on compassion, take off lying and become a teller of truth.

Sin is expelled not by a vacuum but by a stronger affection. And it flows from who you already are — you strip off these sins “seeing that you have put off the old self” (v.9), living out the new man you already are. It is the work of a lifetime, done by the Spirit (Rom. 8:13). So your ongoing struggle is not proof that you have failed or are not truly Christ’s; it is the normal shape of the fight. The old clothes feel familiar and you keep reaching for them, so you keep taking them off, day after day, and God keeps remaking you — progress, not yet perfection (Eph. 4:22–24).

Then Paul names the sins to strip off, and the list travels from the hidden heart out to the open mouth. Anger (orgē) is the settled, smouldering kind — the grudge nursed, the banked fire of resentment that will not go out. Wrath (thymos) is the sudden kind — the flare-up, the outburst that explodes and subsides. Malice is the root beneath both — the ill-will itself, the meanness of spirit that actually wishes another harm. And slander (blasphēmia) is injurious speech that runs a person down. But how do you tell slander from a legitimate warning? — for Scripture itself names real dangers and even real names. Three tests. Is it true?

Is all anger sinful? No. Jesus looked around at the Pharisees with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart (Mark 3:5), and Paul says Be angry and do not sin (Eph 4:26). Anger at real wrong can be righteous. What Paul tells us to put away is the selfish, settled anger that wants to hurt, the kind that sits beside malice and slander.

Slander traffics in falsehood and the exaggeration that makes a tale juicier; a warning is accurate. Is it necessary, for a good end? A warning protects someone from harm; slander only wounds or entertains or makes the speaker look better. And why are you saying it — in love or in malice? A faithful warning is given reluctantly, in love, usually to the person who can do something about it; slander is told with relish, behind the back, to anyone who will listen. Last comes “obscene talk” — foul, shameful speech; and notice how far the list has travelled, from the hidden heart to the open mouth, for the tongue is the drain through which the heart empties (Matt. 12:34).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Do not lie to one another” — one more sin of speech, and not only bald untruths but half-truths, spin, flattery, broken promises, the whole family of deceit. “To one another” presses it home: lying poisons the trust that holds the new community together. The new people of God are a people of truth, for their God is the God of truth and the devil is the father of lies (John 8:44); to deceive is to wear the old father’s likeness, not the new.

And the reason: “you have put off the old self… and have put on the new self.” Both verbs are completed past acts — already, decisively done. The “old self” is not merely a bundle of bad habits but the whole person you used to be in Adam, your old identity under the reign of sin, “with its practices”; Scripture says it was stripped off and crucified with Christ at your conversion (Rom. 6:6).

So the foundational answer is: already done. The old man is not being slowly removed piece by piece; he was taken off once for all, and the daily putting-away of his leftover practices (vv.5, 8) is not the removal of the old self but the living-out of a removal already accomplished. Likewise you have put on the “new self” — the new person you now are in Christ, the new creation (2 Cor. 5:17), your settled identity in union with the risen Lord (and it is corporate, which is why v.11 says the old divisions of race and class now fall away).

Yet that new self, already put on, is not static: the tense now changes to the continuous “is being renewed” — made new day by day, and passive, for God is the one renewing it (2 Cor. 4:16; Rom. 12:2). Here is the answer to the puzzle of “already, or not yet?” — it is both. The decisive change is done (the old off, the new on: your settled identity); the transformation is ongoing (the new self being renewed: your daily growth). This is sanctification, and God himself is at work in it.

It is renewal “in knowledge” — not dry facts, and not the counterfeit secret “knowledge” of the false teachers, but the true, personal knowledge of God (epignōsis), coming to know him as he really is in Christ (2:3); the fall plunged the mind into darkness about God (Rom. 1:21), and this renewal reverses it, for knowing God rightly is itself transforming. And it is “after the image of its creator” — reaching back to Genesis: man was made “in the image of God” (Gen. 1:26–27), the image defaced (though not erased) by the fall, now being restored in Christ, who is himself “the image of the invisible God” (1:15). To be renewed after the Creator’s image is to be conformed to Christ (Rom. 8:29) — God re-stamping his own likeness on the soul.

Put the whole picture together. Coming to Christ was like stripping off filthy, ragged old work clothes and putting on a clean new set — and that change of clothes has already happened, once and for all: you are dressed in the new man. So the daily Christian life is simply to live as the man you now are: keep taking off the scraps of old filthy clothing you still find yourself reaching for, and keep wearing the new. And while you do, God is at work on you like a master restorer cleaning a great portrait that has been painted over and grimed with age — patiently bringing back, stroke by stroke, the original image of the King that the fall had buried.

Is it ever right to lie, for example to protect life, as the Hebrew midwives and Rahab did? Christians have disagreed. Some hold that deceiving those set on murder is not the lying Scripture forbids, since God dealt well with the midwives (Exod 1:20). Others, with Augustine and Calvin, hold that every lie is a sin, though God may honour the faith behind it. The more likely reading is the second, but such cases are rare and extreme. The command here is about the trust among believers: Christians should be people whose word can always be relied on.

You cannot always see the progress, and the cleaning can be slow, but the Master does not abandon a portrait he has begun to restore (Phil. 1:6). So when you still struggle, the answer is not despair but this twofold truth: the decisive change is done (you are the new man, clothed in Christ), and the renewal is under way (God is restoring his image in you). Keep putting off, keep putting on, and leave the renewing to the Restorer (cf. 2 Cor. 3:18).

verseByVerse.quote: Here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This looks like a new topic but is not. Paul has spoken of putting on the new self (vv.9–10); now he says that in this new self the old human divisions disappear. The link is the “new man” — for the new self is not only personal but corporate: Christ is forming a whole new humanity, and in that new people the walls that divide the old humanity no longer stand.

“There is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free.” Paul names the great dividing-lines of his world, across every category — race (Greek and Jew, the deepest divide), religion (circumcised and uncircumcised), culture (a “barbarian” was anyone whose speech sounded like babble to Greek ears, and the Scythian was the byword for the lowest, wildest, most despised of all — Paul deliberately reaches to the most extreme example), and class (slave, free).

Race, religion, culture, class: he sweeps up the whole spectrum of human division, down to the most extreme, to make one point — in the new humanity, none of these any longer defines a person or divides the body. There is no one so foreign, so low, so looked-down-upon that he cannot be one in Christ with anyone else. The walls that structured the entire ancient world (and ours) come down at the foot of the cross — not erased as facts (a Jew is still a Jew, a slave still a slave) but dethroned: they no longer decide a person’s worth, his standing before God, or his place in the family.

And here is the glorious replacement for all those labels: “Christ is all, and in all.” Christ is all — everything, the sum and substance, the one thing that finally counts; in place of the old categories that ranked and divided, there is now a single defining reality. And “in all” — the same Christ lives in every one of his people, Jew or Greek, slave or free, polished or rough, and that indwelling is what makes them one. So three things to take home.

Your worth and identity are no longer measured by what the world ranks people by — nationality, job, class, whether you are “somebody” or “nobody”; the only thing that ultimately defines you is that you belong to Christ and Christ is in you. This makes you truly one with every other believer, however different — richer or poorer, of another race or background — so never let the world’s divisions divide the church. And here is the wonder: the same Christ in whom all the fullness of God dwells (1:19) lives in plain, ordinary you. You are not on the outside of the blessing looking in — Christ is in you (Gal. 3:28; Eph. 2:14–16).
verseByVerse.note: Scythians, from north of the Black Sea, were thought of as the most uncivilised of barbarians.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If the old self is stripped off, the new self must be clothed: “put on.” And Paul roots the command in identity before he names a single virtue — “as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved.” These graces are not a program to earn God’s favour but the wardrobe that suits those who already have it; the beloved can afford to love. So the new self puts on compassion and kindness, true humility (not the self-hating or showy counterfeit of chapter 2) and meekness (strength under control, not weakness), and patience — worked out in the friction of real church life as bearing with one another’s faults and forgiving real wrongs. And the measure of forgiveness is staggering: “as the Lord has forgiven you” — freely, fully, before we ever asked. Over all these is drawn the one garment that holds the rest together: love, the bond of perfect harmony.

From character Paul moves to the community’s shared life, and three things govern it. The peace of Christ is to umpire the heart and the body, making the call when tensions pull the one body apart. The word of Christ is to dwell richly — a resident, not a guest — overflowing into the mutual ministry of teaching and admonishing one another in wisdom, and into psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs that lodge the truth in the heart.

And the whole is summed up in the most sweeping statement of Christ’s lordship in the New Testament: “whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus.” There is no secular corner; the humblest task, done as Christ’s representative and for his honour, becomes worship. And threaded through the entire section — three times in three verses — runs its keynote: thankfulness. The community that puts on the new self is a peace-ruled, Word-saturated, singing, and above all thankful people.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Virtues of the New Self as the Character of Christ

The list of virtues in Colossians 3:12–15 is nothing less than a portrait of Christ himself: compassionate, kind, humble, meek, patient, forgiving, loving, peaceful. Reformed theology understands sanctification as progressive conformity to the image of Christ (Rom 8:29); the virtues Paul commands here are the specific contours of that image. They are not generated by the believer through moral effort; they are produced by the Spirit as the fruit of genuine union with Christ (compare the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22–23). The community that puts on these virtues is the community that is becoming what it already is in Christ: holy and beloved.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian community, like every early Christian community, was a mixture of people from very different backgrounds — Jewish, Greek, slave, free — with very different habits of relating and conflicting. The virtues Paul commands were counter-cultural in every direction: humility was scorned by Graeco-Roman aristocratic culture; forgiveness was a novelty in a world organized around honour and revenge. Now: The church remains the most diverse social reality in the world, and the virtues Paul commands remain equally counter-cultural. The church that is genuinely putting on compassion, kindness, humility, and forbearance will look radically different from any other community the world contains, because these virtues are the character of the one who was raised for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Put on then, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience, bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive. And above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The clothing image continues: having stripped off the old sins (vv.8–9), you now put on the new virtues — you get dressed in the character of Christ. The Christian life is never merely stopping the bad; it is actively clothing yourself with the good, deliberately and daily, the way you put on clothes each morning — choosing to act in compassion, kindness, patience even before the feeling arrives, and very often the feeling follows the action. And Paul names who you are before he names a single virtue: “as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved” — three words, all three God’s prior work on you.

Chosen: he set his love on you and picked you out before you had done anything to deserve it (Eph. 1:4). Holy: set apart as his treasured people. Beloved: dearly loved, sharing the belovedness of his beloved Son (1:13). The identity comes before the commands, and the commands flow from it: you do not put on these graces to become chosen and loved, but because you already are — and a man secure in being loved can afford to pour himself out for others. The beloved can afford to love.

The first garments are tender ones — compassionate hearts (a gut-level pity genuinely moved by another’s pain) and kindness (that compassion turned into action): compassion feels, kindness acts, and it is the very kindness of God that leads us to repentance (Rom. 2:4). Then humility — strikingly, the very word the false teachers twisted into ascetic show (2:18), but here the real thing: a right estimate of yourself before God, knowing you are a sinner saved by sheer grace and therefore not above anyone, that “counts others more significant than yourself” (Phil. 2:3).

It is not thinking you are worthless or wallowing in self-hatred — that is self-absorption with a long face; it is not thinking less of yourself but thinking of yourself less. Then meekness, also misunderstood: not weakness or spinelessness — the Greeks used the word for a wild horse broken and tamed, all its power still there but now under control; meekness is strength under control, the gentleness of one who could retaliate but chooses not to (Jesus was “gentle and lowly,” Matt. 11:29, yet cleansed the temple, John 2:15). And patience — literally “long-tempered,” slow to anger, God’s own patience with us (Rom. 2:4) worn toward others.

Then these virtues meet real life: “bearing with one another” is putting up with each other’s rough edges — the brother who talks too long, the sister always late, the personality that grates — making allowance and overlooking the irritation, the way a family puts up with one another’s annoying habits around the same breakfast table, because they are family. And “forgiving each other, as the Lord has forgiven you” handles the real wrongs: to forgive is to release the debt, refusing the grudge and the revenge, just as God cancelled your own vast debt (2:14) — and the measure is staggering, “as the Lord has forgiven you,” freely, fully, and before you ever asked, while you were still his enemy (Rom. 5:8–10).

So must you forgive only when the other apologizes, or at once? The forgiving heart — the release of bitterness, the readiness and longing to forgive — you must have always, immediately, whether or not the other ever asks (Mark 11:25); you never nurse a grudge until the offender grovels. The full reconciliation — the “I forgive you” spoken and received, the relationship restored — is completed when the other turns and repents (Luke 17:3); restoration, by its nature, takes two. So forgive from the heart at once, holding nothing back, and stand ready, even eager, to fold the other back into fellowship the moment he turns.

Must I seek reconciliation with someone who abused me? Forgiving from the heart means letting go of revenge and handing the wrong to God. It does not mean trusting a dangerous or unrepentant person, resuming contact, keeping the abuse secret, or giving up church discipline or the protection of the law; the state is God’s servant to punish wrongdoing (Rom 13:4). Reconciliation needs repentance and changed behaviour, and safety comes first.

“And above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony.” Love is the crowning garment — the outer robe pulled on over the whole wardrobe. Not mainly a warm feeling or romance (you can love, that is, seek the good of, a person you do not naturally like), but a settled commitment of the will to seek another’s good and give yourself for it, at cost, regardless of merit or return — the love mapped out in 1 Corinthians 13. And why “above all”? Because love is the bond (syndesmos, a ligament — the very picture of 2:19) that ties all the other graces together and ties the whole body together “in perfect harmony.” Without love the rest fall apart and ring hollow (1 Cor. 13:1–3); with love drawn over them all, they are bound into one beautiful, mature character. Love is the thread that holds the entire garment together (cf. John 13:34–35).

verseByVerse.quote: And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in one body. And be thankful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts.” The peace of Christ is the peace he won and gives — the peace he made “by the blood of his cross” (1:20): first, peace with God, the war ended; and out of that, the settled calm he leaves with his people (“my peace I give to you,” John 14:27) and the peace that should reign between them. And “rule” (brabeuetō) is the umpire’s word — the referee who makes the call and settles the contest. So let Christ’s peace be the umpire in your heart: when you are torn or anxious, when relationships are strained, when a decision pulls you two ways, let his peace make the call — refuse what shatters it, choose what preserves it. Do not let anger, fear, or self-will referee your heart; let the peace of Christ do it.

This peace is part of your calling — God did not call you to strife but to peace (1 Cor. 7:15) — and you were called “in one body,” into the one body of Christ (recall v.11, the one new humanity made of every kind of person). So this peace is not merely a private inner calm but the bond meant to govern the body’s life together; you are no lone Christian, and the same peace that umpires your heart is to keep the whole church one. And “be thankful” — a short command, but the first of three calls to thanksgiving in three verses, for gratitude is the keynote of this section. It belongs beside peace, because the thankful heart is the peaceful heart: gratitude crowds out the grumbling and grievance that breed strife and anxiety, and the man counting his mercies has no room to nurse complaints (cf. Phil. 4:6–7).

verseByVerse.quote: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with thankfulness in your hearts to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The word of Christ” — the phrase is rare in Paul (elsewhere only Rom. 10:17), and means the message that is Christ’s, the gospel of which he is the heart, the apostolic teaching about him that the Colossians received (“the word of the truth, the gospel,” 1:5); not narrowly the red-letter sayings alone but the whole word that proclaims him, embracing all of Scripture, which everywhere testifies to him. Note the pointed contrast: let Christ’s word fill you, not the “philosophy and empty deceit” of the false teachers (2:8).

And it is to “dwell in you richly” — “dwell” means to take up residence, to make a home, not to drop by as an occasional visitor; “richly” means abundantly, in full and spacious measure. So the word of Christ is to be a resident, not a guest, furnishing every room of the heart. How? By deep and regular intake — reading, hearing, pondering, memorizing — and by the two channels Paul names next. This is, in fact, how all the putting-off and putting-on actually happens: the mind is renewed (v.10) as the Word takes up rich residence within.

The richly-dwelling Word overflows into a mutual ministry: “teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom.” Teaching is the positive imparting of truth; admonishing is the corrective side — warning and urging a brother away from wrong (the same word Paul used of his own ministry, 1:28). And mark “one another”: this is not the task of the official teachers alone but of every member, ordinary believers ministering the Word to each other — done “in all wisdom,” skillfully and fittingly, with discernment to know what word the moment needs.

Does this mean only the Psalms may be sung in worship? Those who hold to exclusive psalmody point out that all three words are used in the titles of the Greek Psalter, and that only inspired songs are fit for worship. But Paul names three kinds of song, and the New Testament itself contains Christian songs about Christ (Phil 2:6–11; 1 Tim 3:16). The more likely reading is that the church may sing the Psalms and also new songs faithful to Scripture, as long as the word of Christ fills them.

And the third overflow is song: “psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” — psalms (the inspired Old Testament songbook), hymns (songs of praise, perhaps like the great hymn of 1:15–20), and spiritual songs (Spirit-prompted song of every kind); we need not press rigid distinctions, for together they mean the full range of sung worship. Singing is itself a way the Word “dwells richly” and a form of teaching one another (so the parallel in Eph. 5:19) — sung truth lodges in the heart as nothing else does — and it is to be done “with thankfulness in your hearts to God.” Worship is the Word set to music in a thankful heart.

verseByVerse.quote: And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Whatever you do, in word or deed” — the sweeping summary of the whole section, and one of the most comprehensive statements of Christ’s lordship in all of Scripture. “Whatever” — nothing is left out; “in word or deed” — everything you say and everything you do, the two halves that cover the whole of life. Not merely the “religious” parts, but the entire ordinary round — work, family, meals, rest, the chat in the street. There is no secular corner walled off from Christ; the whole of your Monday belongs under this word.

“Do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus.” To act “in someone’s name” is to act as his representative — on his behalf, under his authority, for his honour, in dependence on him, in a way worthy of him. So to do everything in Jesus’ name is to live as his man in all things: to drive the van, pay the bill, speak the word, and do the task as Christ’s representative, for his glory, by his help, in a manner that would not shame his name. This both consecrates the ordinary (the humblest task becomes service of Christ) and constrains the sinful (you cannot do in his name what dishonours it).

Here is the heart of the whole ethical section — not a fence of external rules, as the false teachers wanted (2:20–23), but the lordship of Christ reaching into every word and deed from the inside. And the third call to thanksgiving closes it: everything done in Jesus’ name is wrapped in gratitude to the Father, “through him” — for our thanks, like all our approach to God, comes to the Father through Christ, the one Mediator (the quiet final answer to the angel-mediators of chapter 2: no other channel is needed or allowed). Lordship and gratitude — every word and deed turned into worship (cf. 1 Cor. 10:31; Eph. 5:20).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
With the great doctrine of the new self in place (3:1–17), Paul brings the lordship of Christ home — quite literally — to the household, the ordinary roof under which most of life was lived. He does not tear down the structures of the ancient home; he fills them with a wholly new spirit. The drumbeat of the whole passage is one phrase repeated in varied form — “as is fitting in the Lord,” “fearing the Lord,” “as for the Lord and not for men,” “you also have a Master in heaven.” The risen Christ of chapter 1 is now the governing reality of the breakfast table, the nursery, and the workplace.

And Paul takes the relationships two by two, and — here is the quiet revolution — he addresses not only the subordinate but the one who holds the power, laying a costly command on the strong. Wives are to submit as is fitting in the Lord; husbands are given the harder word — to love sacrificially as Christ loved the church, and never to grow harsh or bitter. Children are to obey, a thing that pleases the Lord and bears the family likeness of the obedient Son who was himself subject at Nazareth (Luke 2:51); fathers are not to provoke and crush their children but to nurture them.

Bondservants are to work heartily, with sincerity of heart, as for the Lord Christ himself — the lowliest labour rendered to the King of kings, and rewarded with an inheritance that no earthly slave could ever receive; and masters, who in that world owed their slaves nothing, are commanded to deal with them justly and fairly. In a culture where the authority of husband, father, and master was absolute, every one of these paired commands to love, nurture, and do justice was startlingly counter-cultural.

None of this is bare rule-keeping. It is the overflow of the gospel just announced: those who have died and been raised with Christ (3:1–3), who do everything “in the name of the Lord Jesus” (3:17), now let that new life reshape the most intimate relationships they have. And running underneath is a great leveller: with the Lord “there is no partiality” (3:25), and even the master “has a Master in heaven” (4:1). At the foot of the cross the husband and wife, parent and child, slave and master kneel side by side as sinners saved by one grace, servants of one Lord. Paul does not, in a sentence, abolish the social order of the Roman world — but he plants within it a seed of love and equality-before-God that, properly cultivated, could never leave that order unchanged.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lordship of Christ in the Household: Sacred and Ordinary

The household code illustrates one of Reformed theology’s most important convictions: there is no sacred-secular divide. The lordship of Christ claimed in the great hymn of chapter 1 arrives in chapter 3 at the level of household management, parenting, and the workplace. Abraham Kuyper’s “every square inch” is not abstract theology; it is the practical implication of “whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus” (3:17). The Christian who is an excellent spouse, a patient parent, and an honest worker is doing theology in the most concrete possible form.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Graeco-Roman household was organized around the absolute authority of the paterfamilias — husband, father, master. Over children and slaves his authority was close to absolute in law. Paul does not abolish this structure but fills it with a different spirit: love, not domination; encouragement, not provocation; justice, not exploitation. The counterpart to every command of submission is a command of love and care that was genuinely counter-cultural. Now: The application of these principles in contemporary household and work relationships continues to produce the same counter-cultural witness: the Christian employee who works with integrity “as to the Lord” even when unsupervised; the Christian employer who treats workers with justice and fairness; the Christian parent who encourages rather than exasperates. Each is a small enactment of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With v.17 Paul said everything is to be done in the name of the Lord Jesus, and now he brings that lordship into the home. “Submit” (hypotassō) means to order or arrange oneself under, and the form is reflexive and voluntary: the wife places herself under, freely. It is not something the husband seizes or imposes; it is her own glad, chosen deference to her husband’s God-given role of loving leadership (the “headship” of Eph. 5:23).

And it is “to your own husbands” — one marriage, not women in general deferring to men in general. Positively, it is a disposition of respect, support, and trust: a wife coming alongside her husband as his partner, honouring and strengthening his leadership rather than competing with it, and — when a real decision must finally be made and they still differ — trusting his lead. Paul even frames it as a reflection of something beautiful: the church’s glad submission to Christ (Eph. 5:24).

And, just as importantly, what it does not mean — for the word is so often abused. It does not mean the wife is inferior: she is fully equal in worth and standing before God, a co-heir of the grace of life (1 Pet. 3:7; Gal. 3:28); submission is a matter of role and order, never of value — just as the Son is fully equal to the Father in deity yet gladly does the Father’s will. It does not mean slavish obedience: tellingly, Paul tells children and slaves to “obey” (vv.20, 22) but tells wives to “submit,” the gentler word. It does not mean silence or having no voice: she is a strong helper and counterpart (Gen. 2:18) who speaks, advises, and may freely disagree — godly women in Scripture did exactly that.

It does not mean obeying into sin: her submission is “in the Lord,” so if a husband demands what God forbids, she must “obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). It is not a licence for harshness or abuse — the very next verse forbids the husband to be harsh, and a wife is nowhere commanded to submit to cruelty or danger; where there is abuse, the church must protect, not preach “submit.” And it is not earned by the husband’s worthiness, nor the submission of all women to all men. In short: a strong, godly, free woman gladly honouring her own husband’s leadership — never a crushed or silenced one.

What does it look like? Most decisions in a healthy marriage are simply made together, by agreement; headship and submission rarely have to “kick in.” But picture the genuine deadlock: they have prayed, talked it through, weighed it honestly — a move, a major purchase, a direction for the family — and still disagree, yet a decision must be made. There the wife trusts and supports her husband’s leading rather than insisting on her own way or making him pay for it.

Egalitarian Christians read this in light of the call to mutual submission (Eph 5:21) and Paul’s statement that in Christ there is no male and female (Gal 3:28), and see the household instructions as tied to the culture of the day. But Paul grounds the husband’s headship in Christ and the church, not in culture (Eph 5:23–25), and he gives husbands a different command: to love, not to submit. The more likely reading is that husbands and wives are equal before God with different callings, the wife’s submission being freely given in the Lord, never a licence for a husband to rule harshly (v. 19).

Day to day it looks like speaking well of him, backing his leadership instead of undercutting it, treating him with genuine respect (Eph. 5:33) — the picture of a Sarah (1 Pet. 3:5–6), a woman of strength who freely honours her husband, not a doormat who has lost her voice. And Paul grounds it not in custom but “as is fitting in the Lord” — which does three things: it dignifies her submission (an act of devotion to Christ, not capitulation to a husband’s superiority), it roots the command in Christ rather than shifting culture, and it limits it — because her submission is “in the Lord,” it can never be a submission that dishonours the Lord. The same phrase that asks it also guards it.

verseByVerse.quote: Husbands, love your wives, and do not be harsh with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Husbands, love your wives” — the word is agapē, not first a romantic glow but the deliberate, self-giving love of the will that seeks the wife’s good (the love crowned in 3:14). Paul states it briefly here; his parallel letter spells out the measure: “love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Eph. 5:25) — nothing less than the sacrificial, self-emptying love of Christ for his people. So the husband’s headship of v.18 is here defined, and it turns out to be headship-by-sacrifice, not headship-by-domination: he leads by giving himself away. And mark how counter-cultural this was — the household codes of the ancient world loaded the duties onto the lesser party and told the husband almost nothing; Paul turns and lays on the man the harder command.

It is a love that is sacrificial (her good above his comfort), constant (a settled commitment, not rising and falling with his feelings or her loveliness on a given day), and active — it “nourishes and cherishes” her as a man cares for his own body (Eph. 5:28–29). It looks like a husband who puts his wife’s good ahead of his own comfort, cherishes and provides and listens, serves her in small unglamorous ways (the Lord himself knelt to wash feet, John 13:5), and keeps loving her on the day she is hardest to love, because his love is a covenant, not a mood. In a word, it looks like Christ.

“And do not be harsh with them” — the word (from pikros, “bitter”) means do not be embittered, do not grow sharp or sour with your wife. Having commanded love, Paul at once names love’s opposite, because it is precisely the husband’s characteristic temptation: the very strength of his position can curdle into domination, and small resentments can harden into a cold, critical spirit toward the one he should cherish most. The present tense warns against the slow settling-in of such a spirit — do not let bitterness take root.

It wears familiar clothes: the cutting tone, the sarcasm, the criticism never satisfied, the contempt, the short temper, the silence used as a weapon, the “winning” of every argument by sheer sharpness. Often it is the strange sin of the man who is gentle and pleasant with everyone else — colleagues, friends, strangers — and saves his harshness for his own wife. The cure is the very character Paul has just commanded: the compassion, kindness, meekness, and patience of 3:12, and the readiness to forgive rather than nurse a grievance until it sours (3:13). A wife was never given to her husband to be a target for his bitterness, but to be loved as Christ loves (cf. 1 Pet. 3:7).

verseByVerse.quote: Children, obey your parents in everything, for this pleases the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Notice that Paul speaks directly to the children — they are real members of the church, able to hear God’s word and answer it. “Obey” means to listen and to do — not merely to feel respect but actively to heed — and it looks different at different ages. For the young child, it is plain, glad, prompt obedience in the daily round: coming when called, doing the chore, going to bed; this is the very nursery of discipleship, where a little one first learns to submit to God by submitting to those God has set over him. For the older child and teenager, the relationship matures but the call remains, now expressed as honour and trust — keeping the household’s rules, receiving correction without rebellion.

And for the grown child who has formed his own household, the word shifts: the duty to obey belongs to the years under the parental roof, but the duty to honour never expires (Eph. 6:2) — the adult child no longer takes orders as a boy did, but never stops respecting, caring for, and providing for his parents as they age (1 Tim. 5:4, 8). Obedience belongs to childhood; honour is lifelong. One needful word on “in everything”: the sweep is wide, but not absolute, for all human authority is held under God’s — the parallel reads “obey your parents in the Lord” (Eph. 6:1), and a child is never bound to obey a parent who commands him to sin (Acts 5:29). But that exception is rare; the plain meaning, for nearly every child on nearly every day, is simply: obey, fully and gladly.

“For this pleases the Lord” — and why does it delight him so? Above all, because in obeying, a child walks in the very footsteps of the Lord Jesus himself, the great obedient Son: “I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38); he was “obedient to the point of death” (Phil. 2:8). And here is the wonder — the eternal Son, by whom all things were made, spent thirty years in a carpenter’s home and “was submissive” to Mary and Joseph (Luke 2:51).

So when a child obeys, he bears the family likeness of the Son who delighted to obey his Father. Two other reasons join it: the obedient home reflects God’s own good order, and the child’s obedience to his parents is, underneath, obedience to God, who set parents over him. Let a child hear it plainly: when you obey, you genuinely bring joy to the heart of God — and you do it not to win his love, but as one who already belongs to the obedient Son (cf. Prov. 1:8–9; Luke 2:51–52).

verseByVerse.quote: Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Fathers, do not provoke your children” — the word means to irritate, exasperate, stir up to resentment; the parallel puts it sharply, “do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (Eph. 6:4). Here, as with the husband and the master, the one who holds the power is given the restraining word: a father’s strength is to build his children up, never to crush them. Fathers exasperate their children in a hundred ways — by harshness and a never-satisfied criticism, by unfairness and favouritism, by punishing in temper, by impossible expectations, by domineering control, by hypocrisy (demanding what he will not do himself), and by cold neglect that withholds all warmth and praise. The good way is the opposite of every one: patient, warm, consistent nurture that disciplines and encourages, and points the child to Christ.

It looks different across the years. A young child is provoked by impatience and a sharp tongue over ordinary childish failings — the spilled cup, the mess — by anger out of all proportion, by rules that change with the father’s mood, by promises lightly broken; the good way is gentleness, clear boundaries held with warmth, generous affection and praise, expectations fitted to his age. The school-age child is provoked by constant criticism, by being compared to a sibling, by praise that never comes, by mockery and shaming; the good way is to encourage and to notice — specific praise for honest effort, real interest in his world, discipline that is fair and explained.

The teenager is provoked by a control that will not loosen as he grows, by being treated as a little boy, by endless lecturing, by belittling, by “because I said so” where a reason was owed; the good way is to let trust and responsibility grow together, to listen and reason, to choose the battles that matter, to keep the relationship warm, to own his own faults, and above all to point the young person to Christ, not merely enforce a rulebook. Even a grown child can be provoked by a father who still dictates and criticises his choices, his spouse, his way of raising his own children; the good way now is to honour the child’s adulthood — to advise when asked, to bless rather than control.

And note how the discouragement shows at each stage: a bruised little heart in tears and timidity; a school child who gives up trying (“why bother — I’ll never be good enough for him”), grows sullen, and quietly stops bringing his small joys to his father; a teen whose discouragement erupts as open rebellion or — just as dangerous — sinks into withdrawal, secrecy, and a deadened, joyless compliance.

Through every stage one pattern holds, set by the gospel: the earthly father is to father as God fathers his own — “as a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him” (Ps. 103:13). God disciplines, but never crushes; he is firm yet tender, the Father from whom all fatherhood takes its name (Eph. 3:14–15). And the Christian father parents not to earn anything, but out of the fullness of a man who is himself a dearly loved child of that Father — passing on to his children the very grace he has received (cf. Heb. 12:7–11).

verseByVerse.quote: Bondservants, obey in everything those who are your earthly masters, not by way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. You are serving the Lord Christ. For the wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong he has done, and there is no partiality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word for “bondservants” is doulos, slave. Slavery ran right through the Roman world — a large share of the empire’s population — but it was not the race-based chattel slavery of later centuries: people became slaves by capture in war, by birth, or by selling themselves to escape debt, and many were educated, held some money, and could in time be freed. So it was harsh and varied, not a permanent doom. (Paul is not blessing the system; elsewhere he quietly undermines it — “if you can gain your freedom, do so,” 1 Cor. 7:21; and in Christ master and slave are brothers, as the letter to Philemon shows. He is teaching believers how to live for Christ inside a system the gospel would in time dissolve.) The how-to-work of these verses carries straight across to any modern job; the conditions do not.

“Obey in everything those who are your earthly masters” — the full scope of the master’s lawful direction, done thoroughly, not just the pleasant parts (with the unspoken limit that governs all such obedience: never into sin, for the Lord outranks every master). And mark the exact phrase: “earthly masters” is literally “masters according to the flesh” — in a single phrase Paul puts the human master in his place; he is your master only on the passing, earthly level, and you have a greater Master above him.

So work “not by way of eye-service, as people-pleasers” — “eye-service” (a word Paul seems to have coined) is work that only happens while the master’s eye is on you, busy when watched and idle when his back is turned; the people-pleaser works to impress the man. It is one of the oldest temptations of the workplace and has not aged a day — the employee who looks busy when the manager passes and slacks when he is gone, who games the metrics for the review. The gospel has no room for “as long as nobody is looking,” because Someone always is.

Against all that, work “with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord” — an undivided heart, the same whether watched or not, in awe of the Lord who is always watching. Here is the great turn: you work well not because the master deserves it, not because he happens to be watching, but because you stand in awe of the Lord whose will this is. Even a slave with a cruel and thankless master serves with all his heart — not for the master’s sake at all, but for the Lord’s. The audience of your work has changed: it is no longer the boss; it is God.

So “whatever you do, work heartily” — the Greek is vivid, work “from the soul,” putting your whole self in, not grudgingly or by halves, sparing nothing, not the menial or dreary or unseen task — “as for the Lord and not for men.” Here is why drudgery becomes worship: you are not, in the end, working for the man who signs your orders but for the Lord; Christ is your true Master, and every task is handed, as it were, directly to him. The earthly master may be unworthy, ungrateful, even cruel — it does not finally matter, because he is not the one you are ultimately serving. Hand the swept floor to Jesus, and a mean master cannot rob it of its glory (Eph. 6:7).

Now feel the force of the promise: “from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward.” Under Roman law a slave could not inherit — inheritances went to sons, never to slaves. Yet Paul promises this slave the inheritance, the whole eternal estate of God’s people (1:12), “imperishable… kept in heaven for you” (1 Pet. 1:4). The man who owns nothing and can inherit nothing on earth is a full heir of God: he may get no wage, no thanks, no advancement from his earthly master, but the Lord sees and will repay, not with coins but with glory.

(The inheritance is not wages earned — you receive it as a son, by grace; the “reward” is God graciously crowning the very service his own grace enabled.) And here is the clincher: “you are serving the Lord Christ.” When the believing slave does his master’s bidding, he is in reality rendering that service to Christ — the lowliest labour, done in faith, rises to the King of kings as service offered to him (Matt. 25:40). There is no higher title in the universe. And Paul adds a warning that reaches both ways — “the wrongdoer will be paid back… and there is no partiality”: to the slave, do not imagine your low place lets you get away with lazy or spiteful work; to the master (whom 4:1 turns to address), the one who wrongs his servant will not escape. God plays no favourites; he weighs the deed, not the rank, so the powerless need not fear that the powerful will buy their way out (Rom. 2:11).

Now bring it into your own world. You are no slave, but you have a boss, a job, and a great heap of work that is repetitive, unseen, and rarely thanked — and watch what this does to your Monday. The cleaner mopping an empty corridor, the clerk filling the same forms, the carer washing a body no one else will touch — when it is done “for the Lord,” it is laid into the hands of the King who flung the stars into space and bled upon a cross. Your foreman may never say thank you; the Lord is keeping account, and forgets nothing.

No task is too small to be worship, no worker too low to be Christ’s honoured servant, no good hour ever truly unseen. And here is the wonder that should raise the hair on the back of the neck: the servant who owns nothing, who is invisible to the great of this world, is the servant of the Lord Christ and the heir of all things. The drudgery turns to glory; the overlooked man is the honoured one. And you do none of it to earn Christ — you are already his, already an heir — but as a beloved son carrying his clumsy day’s work up to a Father who is delighted to receive it. Whatever you do, do it for him (cf. 1 Cor. 15:58).
verseByVerse.note: One of the slaves in the church was Onesimus, returning to his master in Colossae with this letter.
